<meta>This page begins the Introduction to the translation of the "Saddharma-pundarîka" (the Lotus Sutra), identifying it as one of the nine major Buddhist scriptures of the Nepalese tradition and discussing its literary form.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION.

The *Saddharma-pundarîka* <note>Sanskrit: "The Lotus of the Good Law," one of the most influential scriptures in Mahayana Buddhism.</note> is one of the nine scriptures <note>original: "Dharmas"</note> which are known by the following titles:
1. *Ashtasâhasrikâ Pra-gñâpâramitâ* <note>The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.</note>
2. *Gandavyûha* <note>The Flower Ornament Scripture.</note>
3. *Dasabhûmîshvara* <note>The Scripture of the Ten Stages.</note>
4. *Samâdhi-râga* <note>The King of Meditative Concentrations.</note>
5. *Lankâvatâra* <note>The Descent into Lanka.</note>
6. *Saddharma-pundarîka* <note>The Lotus of the Good Law.</note>
7. *Tathâgata-guhyaka* <note>The Secret of the Thus-Come One (the Buddha).</note>
8. *Lalita-vistara* <note>The Play in Full, a biography of the Buddha.</note>
9. *Suvarnaprabhâsa* <note>The Golden Light Scripture.</note>

These nine works, to which divine worship is offered, encompass (to use the words of Brian Houghton Hodgson, the first investigator of Nepalese Buddhism <note>Hodgson (1800–1894) was a British diplomat and scholar who collected many Sanskrit manuscripts in Nepal.</note>):

> "In the first, a summary of Buddhist philosophy <note>Since the 'Perfect Wisdom' is viewed as the mother of all Buddhas <note>original: "Tathâgatas"</note>, Bodhisattvas, and disciples, we must conclude that this work is primarily intended to explain the fundamental principles of things <note>original: "principia rerum"</note>. It begins with the primordial matter <note>original: "pradhâna" or "pragñâ"</note>, which is why it is placed at the beginning of the list. We might best describe it as a summary of mystical-natural or materialistic philosophy.</note>; in the seventh, a treatise on secret <note>original: "esoteric"</note> doctrines; and in the remaining seven, a full illustration of every point of the ordinary doctrine and discipline. These are taught in an easy and effective way through examples and anecdotes, interspersed with occasional instances of dogmatic instruction. With the exception of the first, these works are therefore of a narrative kind, though they are interwoven with much occasional speculative matter."

Regarding their form, it appears that all these scriptures <note>original: "Dharmas"</note> may be classified as narrative works. However, this does not prevent some of them from having a total difference in style of composition and character. For example <note>original: "e.g."</note>, the *Lalita-vistara* has the movement of a true epic poem, whereas the *Saddharma-pundarîka* does not. The latter has the character of a dramatic performance—an undeveloped "mystery play" <note>A type of medieval drama that depicted religious stories.</note> in which the chief speaker is not the only person involved.

<summary>This page introduces the Lotus Sutra as one of nine foundational Nepalese Buddhist scriptures and discusses its classification as a narrative or dramatic work rather than a traditional epic.</summary>
<keywords>Saddharma-pundarîka, Lotus Sutra, Nine Dharmas, B. H. Hodgson, Buddhist philosophy, Mahayana scriptures, Buddhist literature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the "Saddharma-pundarîka" (the Lotus Sutra), specifically discussing the role of Shakyamuni (the Buddha), the text's classification as a "Great Expanded" (Mahavaipulya) scripture, and its likely date of composition based on historical references to currency.</meta>

<header>SADDHARMA-PUṆDARĪKA.</header>

...one <note>This refers to the primary figure of the text.</note>, is Shakyamuni, the Lord. The text consists of a series of dialogues, brightened by the magical effects of a supernatural setting. The fantastical <note>original: "phantasmagorical"</note> parts of the whole are clearly intended to impress us with the idea of the Buddha's power and glory, just as his speeches are meant to display his all-surpassing wisdom. There is a visible similarity in its technical structure to that of traditional Indian drama, especially in the prologue <note>original: "Nidâna"</note>. In this opening, Manjushri <note>The Bodhisattva of wisdom.</note> prepares the spectators and listeners—who are one and the same—for the beginning of the grand drama by telling them that the Lord is about to awake from his mystic slumber to display his infinite wisdom and power.

Within the book itself, we find it classified as a *Sutra* <note>A scriptural discourse.</note> or *Sutranta* of the class called *Mahavaipulya* <note>Sanskrit: "Great Expanded" sutras, a category of longer, more complex Mahayana texts.</note>. In a highly instructive discussion on the unique characteristics and relative age of different types of Sutras, the scholar Burnouf <note>Eugène Burnouf (1801–1852), a pioneering French scholar of Buddhism.</note> concludes that the *Mahavaipulya Sutras* were written later than the simple Sutras in general.¹ There are two categories of simple Sutras:
1. Those in which the narrated events are set during the lifetime of the Buddha.
2. Those which refer to people living a considerable time after his reported death, such as Emperor Ashoka.²

It follows that the composition of the *Mahavaipulya Sutras* must have occurred even later than the production of the second category of simple Sutras. For instance, in one of the latter, the *Asoka-Avadana* <note>The Legend of Ashoka.</note>, we read of Ashoka using the word *dinara* <note>original: "dînâra"; a gold coin name derived from the Roman "denarius".</note>.³ This leads us to the conclusion that this specific *Avadana* was composed not only after the *dinara* was introduced from the West in the first century AD or later, but at an even more modern time, when people had forgotten that the coin was originally foreign.

The results reached by Burnouf may be correct regarding any *Mahavaipulya Sutra* as a whole; however, they cannot be applied to every component part of such a work. Without looking further than the *Saddharma-pundarîka* itself...

¹ *Introduction to the History of Indian Buddhism* <note>original: "Introduction à l'histoire du Buddhisme indien"</note>, pp. 103-128.
² Burnouf, *Introduction*, p. 218 and following.
³ Burnouf, *Introduction*, p. 423; see also p. 431, where Pushyamitra <note>An emperor of the Shunga Empire (c. 185–151 BC).</note> is made to speak of *Dinaras*; Max Müller, *History of Ancient Sanskrit Literature*, p. 245.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the "Saddharma-pundarîka," focusing on the textual history and composition of Buddhist scriptures. It compares the *Lalita-vistara* and the *Mahâvaipulya Sûtras* to older Pâli texts to demonstrate that these later works incorporate much older source material.</meta>

<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

and the *Lalita-vistara*, it can hardly be questioned that these works contain parts from very different dates and are derived from various sources. The significant discrepancies between the prose and verse versions are occasionally too great to allow us to suppose that they were made at the same time, or even by different authors working together <note>See, for example, the footnote on page 413.</note>. Furthermore, it can be shown that the *Mahâvaipulya Sûtras* are partially made up of materials that must be attributed to the oldest period of Buddhism. Let me provide some examples to clarify what I mean.

If we compare the *Lalita-vistara* (Calcutta edition), page 513, line 13 to page 514, line 2, with the *Mahâvagga* (edited by Dr. Oldenberg) I, 5, 2, we see that the passages are largely identical word-for-word, and that the variations amount to little more than a variation in reading <note>Latin: *varietas lectionis*</note>.

The passage cited is in prose; now let us look at some stanzas. In *Mahâvagga* I, 5, 3, the Lord utters the following verses <note>slokas</note>:

> kikkhena me adhigatam *halam* dâni pakâsitum,
> râgadosaparetehi *nâyam* dhammo susambudho.
> patisotagâmi *nipunam* gambhîram duddasam *anum*
> râgarattâ na dakkhanti tamokhandhena âvutâ.

This does not significantly differ from *Lalita-vistara*, page 515, line 16 and following:

> pratisrotagâmiko mârgo gambhîro durdriso mama,
> na *tam drakshya(n)ti* <note>An incorrect Sanskritization of the present tense *dakkhanti*.</note> râgândhâ *alam* tasmât prakâsitum.
> *anusrotam* pravâhyante kâmeshu patitâh pragâh ;
> *krikkhrena me’yam* samprâptam(!) *alam* tasmât prakâsitum.

Though there is some difference in the wording and arrangement of the verses, it is of such a kind as to exclude the idea that the compiler of the *Lalita-vistara* composed the couplets himself. Even the words *ayam dhammo susambudho* and *nipunam* of the Pâli text were known to him, as appears from the prose passage immediately preceding the verses <note>slokas</note> quoted: *gambhîrah*

<summary>The author argues that Buddhist texts like the Lalita-vistara are compilations of older materials, evidenced by prose and verse passages that are nearly identical to earlier Pâli scriptures. Significant differences between prose and verse versions of the same stories suggest they were composed by different authors at different times.</summary>

<header>SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA.</header>

*khalv ayam, Mahâbrahman, mayâ dharmo 'bhisam-buddhaḥ sûkshmo nipuṇaḥ.* What follows, *api kâme, Brahman, ime gâthe abhîkshṇam pratibhâsataḥ <note>Obviously an unsuccessful attempt to Sanskritize a Pâli or Prâkrit *patibhamsu*; it should have been *pratyabhâsishṭâm*.</note>*, is only a slight and not very successful modification of what we read in the *Mahâvagga* in the place cited: *api 'ssu bhagavantam imâ anakkhariyâ gâthâyo paṭibhamsu pubbe assuta-pubbâ.*

The verses in *Trishṭubh* meter uttered by the god Brahma in *Mahâvagga* I, 5, 7, and those found in the *Lalita-vistara*, page 517, line 3 and following, are evidently from the same source. The former text says:

> *pâturahosi Magadhesu pubbe*
> *dhammo asuddho samalehi kintito,*
> *apâpur' etam amatassa dvâram*
> *sunantu dhammam vimalenânubuddham <note>The text is corrupted; we must read it either as *vimalânubuddham*, a Tatpurusha compound expressing the same thing the text shows, or as *vimalena buddham*.</note>.*

The other version runs as follows:

> *vâdo babhûva samalair vikintito*
> *dharmo hy <note>*Hi* is meaningless and is only a clumsy device to satisfy the requirements of Sanskrit phonetic rules, which do not apply to Prâkrit.</note> asuddho Magadheshu pûrvam;*
> *amṛitam mune tad vivṛinîshva dvâram*
> *sṛinvanti <note>Should read *sṛinvantu*.</note> dharma vipulam <note>Should read *dharmam vimalena*. *Vipula* probably originates from a transcription error (dittography).</note> vimalena buddham.*

On comparing the two texts, we may infer that the Pâli version is purer, and that *vâdo babhûva* is a corruption of *pâdû babhûva* or something similar, corresponding to a Sanskrit *prâdur babhûva*; but we cannot deny that the stanzas have the same origin.

In *Mahâvagga* I, 5, 12, the Lord addresses the god Brahma with the following *Trishṭubh*:

> *apârutâ tesam amatassa dvârâ*
> *ye sotavanto, pamuñkantu <note>I do not understand this *pamuñkantu*, meaning "let them cast off, loose, or emit." Perhaps we should read *payuñgantu*, meaning "let them practice."</note> saddham.*

<summary>This page provides a linguistic comparison of Buddhist verses from the Mahâvagga and Lalita-vistara, arguing that the Sanskrit versions are often clumsy modifications of older Pâli or Prâkrit sources.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION.

Then in prose: Atha kho Brahmâ Sahampati katâvakâso kho 'mhi bhagavatâ dhammadesanâyâ 'ti bhagavantam abhivâdetvâ padakkhinam katvâ tatth' ev' antaradhâyi.

The parallel passage in the *Lalita-vistara*, page 520, line 19 and following, has:

> apâvṛitâs teshâm <gloss>1</gloss> amṛitasya dvârâ
> Brahmann iti <gloss>2</gloss> satatam ye srotavantaḥ,
> praviṣanti śraddhâ na viheṭhasaññâ

Atha khalu Sikhî Mahâbrahmâ Tathâgatasyâdhivâsanaṃ viditvâ tushṭa udagra âttamanâ pramuditaḥ prîtisaumanasyagâtas Tathâgatasya pâdau śirasâbhivanditvâ tatraivântaradhât.

At the meeting of the Âgîvaka monk Upaka and the Buddha, the latter is described as having pronounced the following <term>slokas</term> (*Mahâvagga* I, 6, 8 and 9):

> na me âkariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati,
> sadevakasmim lokasmim n' atthi me paṭipuggalo.
> aham hi arahâ loke, aham satthâ anuttaro,
> eko 'mhi sammâsambuddho, sîtibhûto 'smi nibbuto.
> mâdisâ ve *Ginâ* honti ye pattâ âsavakkhayam,
> *gitâ* me pâpakâ dhammâ tasmâham Upaka <gloss>3</gloss> *gino*.

Essentially the same <term>slokas</term>, although in a somewhat different arrangement, occur in the *Lalita-vistara*, page 526, line 22 and following, as being spoken at the same meeting:

> *âkâryo nahi me kaścit, sadṛiśo me na vidyate,*
> *eko 'ham asmi sambuddhaḥ, sîtibhûto nirâsravaḥ.*
> *aham evâham* <gloss>4</gloss> *loke śâstâ hy aham anuttaraḥ,*
> *sadevâsuragandharve nâsti me pratipudgalaḥ* <gloss>5</gloss>.

An important passage regarding the divine sight of the Buddha in the *Lalita-vistara*, page 439 onwards, occurs almost literally in the *Sâmaññaphala-Sutta*, as has been pointed out by Burnouf³.

These few examples I have chosen will be sufficient to prove that the material of a *Mahâvaipulya Sûtra* is partly as old as that of any other sacred book of the Buddhists. The language of the prose part of those *Sûtras* does not differ from that used in the simple *Sûtras* of the Northern canon. Should the Sanskrit text prove to be younger than the Pâli text, then we may say that we do not possess the Northern tradition in its original form. That result, however, provides no criterion for the distinction between the simple *Sûtras* and the *Mahâvaipulya Sûtras*, for both are written in the very same Sanskrit, if we except the *Gâthâs*.

It would lead me too far were I to enter into the heart of the question regarding which of the three idioms—Sanskrit, Pâli, and the so-called *Gâthâ* dialect—was the oldest scriptural language of the Buddhists; I will therefore confine myself to a few remarks. ...that the same person cannot have uttered any speech or stanza in two languages at the same time, and, furthermore, that he is unlikely to have spoken Sanskrit when expressing himself in prose while resorting to a mere dialect when speaking in poetry. One does not need to assume that the common, everyday language of the god Brahma and the Buddha was Pâli or Prâkrit to find it absurd that these figures would have spoken prose in Sanskrit and poetry in the Gâthâ dialect, as we find in some previously quoted passages and many others. Nor is it absurd—even if we do not believe that Pâli is the original language of scripture—to argue that the Sanskrit text of the canonical works is, at the very least, a translation from some dialect. If the Sanskrit text of the Northern Sûtras were generally the original version, it would be impossible to account for occasional mistranslations or for the fact that the most obvious dialect forms have been left untouched whenever Sanskritizing the passage would have ruined it. 

A striking instance is found in the *Lalita-vistara*, p. 145. There we read that the pronunciation of the letter *tha* of the Indian alphabet is linked to the word *thapanîyaprasna*—that is, a question that should be avoided or set aside (Pâli *thapanîyapañho*). Here, the context completely prevented the Pâli or Prâkrit word *thapanîya* from being translated into the Sanskrit *sthâpanîya*, because the first syllable of the Sanskrit form could not be made to match the letter *tha*. On the same page of the *Lalita-vistara*, we also find the word *airapatha*<note>Written as *âirapatha*, because the *Vriddhi* vowel originally denoted the sound of *âi* in Sanskrit; since the same diphthong is used in the Asoka edicts in the word *thaira* (Sanskrit *sthavira*), we must infer that in the Prâkrit of that time, the diphthong was pronounced *ai*, not *âi*.</note>, the first syllable of which must harmonize with the diphthong *ai*. Consequently, *airapatha* could not be Sanskritized into *âryapatha*. From the occurrence of this *airapatha*, I infer that the original text was composed in some type of *Prâkrit*, rather than regular Pâli, because Pâli has lost both the primary and secondary diphthong *ai*—though it may be asked whether forms such as *kayira* (Sanskrit *kârya*) or *payirupâsati*...

(Sanskrit *paryupâsati*), and similar words are nothing other than instances of inaccurate spelling<note>That is, *kayira* was probably pronounced *kăira*, which cannot be exactly expressed by the character कै, because those who were acquainted with the rules of Sanskrit grammar would pronounce this and similar words with the sound of *âi*.</note>. It is certain that *thaira* occurs in the inscriptions of *Asoka*, and in these the diphthong must have the value of a short *a* followed by *i*.

If we eliminate Sanskrit, two dialects remain: *Pâli* and the *Gâthâ* idiom. Which of the two can claim to be the original language of the Buddhist scriptures, or is the nearest approach to it? *Pâli* is intelligible in its phonetics, while the *Gâthâs* are not. Under ordinary circumstances, the comparatively greater regularity of *Pâli* would tend to favor its claims; however, the case before us is so peculiar that it is not safe to draw inferences from the state in which the *Gâthâs* have come down to us. It seems to me that the verses in the Northern books in general, as well as the prose of the *Mahâvastu*<note>The able editor of this work, M. Senart, makes the following remarks on its language (p. xii): "We are here in the presence of an irregular and unstable language, a singular mixture of diverse forms of age and origin."</note>, have been Sanskritized to a large extent, so that they ought to be restored, as much as possible, to a more primitive form before a comparison with *Pâli* can lead to satisfactory results. When we come across such words as *heshthâd* (Sanskrit *adhastâd*), *gunebhih*, etc., we easily perceive that these forms are more primitive than the *Pâli* *hetthâ* and *gunehi*; but what proof do we have that such forms were really in use at the time when the *Gâthâs* were composed, if we observe that in a verse in the *Lalita-vistara* (page 53), the syllable *bhih* is reckoned as a short one in the words *gunebhih pratipûrna*? In short, in their present state, the *Gâthâs* provide no conclusive evidence that the language in which they were composed is older than *Pâli*.

Whatever the phonetic aspect of the oldest standard dialect of the Buddhists may have been, its vocabulary is unmistakably and closely related to that of the *Satapatha-brâhmana*. The coincidences are so striking that the

Perhaps the most curious of similar forms in the Gâthâs is *ko*, which in meaning exactly coincides with *ka*; I take this *ko* to be the older form of the Mâgadhî *ku* found in the Asoka edicts.

which we wish to determine, has been carefully molded upon time-honored models. In such a case, new words prove a great deal¹, while old ones prove almost nothing. Therefore, it would be an abuse of the argument *ex silentio* <note>An argument based on silence or the lack of contrary evidence.</note> to infer from the total absence of such new words in our *Saddharma-pundarîka* that the bulk of the *Sûtra* must date from the earlier period of Buddhism.

I have already had occasion to notice that the two versions—the prose and the metrical one—in our *Sûtra* show significant discrepancies here and there. The question arises as to which of the two we must award the prize for priority. Repeatedly, in both prose and poetry, the *Sûtra* is spoken of as consisting of stanzas; for example, in chapter vii, stanza 82, and several times in the prose portions of chapters x and xxii. As the term for stanza (*gâthâ*), as far as I know, is never used to denote a specific number of syllables, there is a strong presumption that the ancient text consisted of verses, with an admixture of short prose passages serving as introductions or to connect the more solemn poetical pieces. The idea of expanding such passages into a regular prose version would especially recommend itself at a period when the poetical dialect began to become obsolete and obscure. Without being a formal commentary, the prose version would still tend to clarify the older holy text.

It will not be objected that, because not all chapters in the *Saddharma-pundarîka* have a poetical version added, the original cannot have been a poem. For the chapters containing only one version—namely, xxi, xxii, xxiii, xxv, and xxvi—show decided traces of being later additions; and as to the final chapter, it may be held to be a moderate expansion of a short prose epilogue.

In contending that the original text of our *Sûtra* was probably, in the main, a work in metrical form, I do not mean to say that the poetical version in all the chapters must be

### INTRODUCTION.
<sig>b 2</sig>

---

considered to be older than the prose <note>1. Isolated stanzas, such as those in chapters xxii, xxv, and elsewhere, are completely excluded from this consideration.</note>. The Gâthâs of the *Saddharma-pundarîka* are nowhere particularly brilliant, but in some chapters they are so excessively clumsy and mechanically put together that we are instinctively led to the assumption that they were created by people to whom the old dialect was no longer familiar. The stanzas, for example in chapters xi and xiv, are abominable in form and unusually silly; those in chapter xxiv are a pattern of mechanical verse-making, and give the impression that they were intended more to confuse than to enlighten the credulous reader. Now, it is an interesting fact that in a Chinese preface to the translation of our *Sûtra* by Gñânagupta and Dharmagupta, A.D. 601 <note>2. Catalogue of the Tripitaka (Oxford), by Mr. Bunyiu Nanjio; *Sûtra Pitaka*, column 45.</note>, we find the following notice: ‘The omission of the Gâthâs in No. 134, chapters 12 and 25 <note>3. In the English translation, chapters xi and xxiv.</note>, has since been filled in by some wise men, whose example I wish to follow <note>4. Another notice in the above-mentioned Catalogue, column 44, states: ‘The prose portion’ (of chapter xxiv) ‘was translated by Kumâragîva, of the later Tshin dynasty, A.D. 384–417; and that of the Gâthâs by Gñânagupta, of the Northern Keu dynasty, A.D. 557–589.’ So it seems that the Gâthâs were added, and quite likely composed, between 417 and 557 A.D.</note>.’

Here we have direct proof that the Gâthâs of some chapters were added in later times. If we had similar notices concerning all the chapters in which the Gâthâs are of a relatively modern date, and if we could prove that the prose of such chapters belongs to a later period, then the theory that the ancient text of the *Saddharma-pundarîka* was mainly a metrical one would seem to lose its weight. For, reasoning by analogy, one might say that just as some later chapters have famously been expanded with a metrical version in later times, so the ancient parts also would have gradually received their Gâthâs. Still, the fact remains that those chapters in which the metrical portion is missing clearly belong to a later period, so it is doubtful whether their situation is entirely similar to that of the more ancient part of the whole work.

<page-num>XX</page-num>
<header>SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA.</header>

At present, we are far from the ultimate goal that critical research must reach; we are not yet able to assign each part of our Sûtra to its proper place in the development of Buddhist literature. We may feel that compositions from different eras have been collected into a whole that is not very harmonious; we may even be able to prove that some passages are as clearly ancient as others are modern, but any attempt to analyze this composite work and reveal its individual parts would seem to be premature. Under these circumstances, the inquiry into the date of the work resolves itself into the question of when the book took its current shape.

It is well known that there exist various Chinese translations of the Saddharma-pundarîka, or parts of it, the dates of which are well established. The previously mentioned catalogue by Mr. Bunyiu Nanjio provides some valuable information on the subject, from which I take the following details <note>1. Sûtra Piṭaka, column 44 and following.</note>:

The oldest Chinese translation, known by the title of *Kan-fâ-hwâ-king*, is by *Ku Fâ-hu* (Dharmaraksha) of the Western Tsin dynasty, A.D. 265–316; it consists of 28 chapters <note>2. In S. Beal, The Buddhist Tripiṭaka, p. 14, the author's name *Ku Fâ-hu* (Chu-fa-hu) is identified as Dharmagupta.</note>.

An incomplete translation titled *Sâ-thân-fan-tho-li-king*, by an unknown author, is equally old.

Next in chronological order is the *Miâo-fâ-lien-hwâ-king* by Kumâragîva, of the later Tshin dynasty, A.D. 384–417 <note>3. Compare Beal, Buddhist Tripiṭaka, p. 15.</note>. It matches the Tibetan version and contains 28 chapters. For one chapter (chapter 24 in the Nepalese manuscripts and the English translation), Kumâragîva translated only the prose; the Gâthâs were rendered by *Gñânagupta* of the Northern *Keu* dynasty, A.D. 557–589.

The final translation in chronological order, titled *Thien-phin-miâo-fâ-lien-hwâ-king*, is by *Gñânagupta* and Dharmagupta, A.D. 601, of the Sui dynasty; it consists of 27 chapters.

We see that the older translations—and, consequently, their original sources—contained one more chapter than our manuscripts.

A look at this table is enough to convince us that chapters 21–26 (1–6) are later additions, if we bear in mind that the order of the chapters down to the Dhâranîs is the same in all sources. This result is quite in harmony with what we would have guessed based on internal evidence. The last chapter, titled Dharmaparyâya, must, by its very nature, have been the conclusion or the epilogue of the whole. In the Chinese translation by *Kumâragîva* it occurs, as the table shows, immediately after chapter 20; this in itself is a clear indication that chapters 21–26 are later additions. It is somewhat strange that in the older translation by *Ku Fâ-hu* the Dharmaparyâya has already taken its place after the additional material, but this may be explained by the theory that *Kumâragîva*, though living at a later time, used ancient manuscripts <note>1. it may be, I think that the following facts can be considered established, based on both internal and external evidence:
1. The more ancient text of the *Saddharma-pundarîka* contained 21 chapters and an epilogue—that is, the content of chapters i–xx and of chapter xxvii; 2. The later additions, probably excepting some verses, had been connected with the work as *Parisishṭas* <note>Addenda</note> about 250 A.D. or earlier. Since the book, along with the *Parisishṭas*, already existed some time before 250 A.D., we may safely conclude that the more ancient text in 21 chapters, including the epilogue, dates several centuries earlier. Greater precision is currently impossible.

We know that a commentary on the *Saddharma-pundarîka* was composed by Vasubandhu <note>Wassiljew, *Buddhism*, p. 222. This was written before my Cambridge Lectures, ‘*India, what can it teach us?*’ were published, and it provides valuable confirmation—because it is independent—of the chronological system found in Note G, ‘*Renaissance of Sanskrit Literature*,’ pp. 281–366.—The Editor, F. M. M.</note>. The date of that work, which has not yet been recovered, it seems, must fall between 550 and 600 A.D., or at least not much earlier; for Vasubandhu's pupil Guṇaprabha became the Guru <note>teacher</note> of the famous Srî-Harsha, also known as Sîlâditya, king of Kanauj and friend of Hiouen Thsang <note>Wassiljew, *Buddhism*, p. 78; compare pp. 64 and 219; Târanâtha, *History of Buddhism* (translated by Schiefner), p. 126.</note>. The latter often mentions Vasubandhu and some of that great doctor's writings, as well as Guṇaprabha <note>See especially *History of the Life of Hiouen Thsang*, pp. 83, 93, 97, 114, 106.</note>. As both notable scholars had already passed away at the time of Hiouen Thsang's visit to India, and as Vasubandhu must have been at least one generation older than Guṇaprabha, we cannot be far wrong in assigning the date specified above to Vasubandhu's commentary.

It appears from the previously mentioned preface to the Chinese translation of 601 A.D. that the textual differences in the manuscripts common in those days were more significant than those we observe in the Nepalese manuscripts from 1000 A.D. onward, with which the Tibetan versions closely agree. Besides these, there are minor differences between the text and translation. The omissions of the Gâthâs in No. 134, chapters 12 and 25, have since been filled in by some wise men, whose example I wish to follow. According to the opinion of an eminent Chinese scholar, the late <term>Stanislas Julien</term>, the translation by <term>Kumâragîva</term> differs widely from <term>Burnouf’s</term>. On comparing the fragment with the corresponding passages in <term>Burnouf’s</term> French translation and the English version in this volume, the reader will certainly notice that the discrepancies between the two European versions are fewer and less significant than those between either of them and <term>Kumâragîva’s</term> work. It is unlikely that the text used by <term>Kumâragîva</term> could have differed so much from ours; it seems far more probable that he took the liberty, for the sake of clarity, to modify the structure of the verses—a literal translation of which, it must be admitted, is impossible in any language. It is a pity that <term>Stanislas Julien</term> chose for his sample a fragment consisting exclusively of <term>Gâthâs</term>. A page in prose would have been far more useful as a test of the accuracy of the Chinese version.

I have no objection to this, but I do have something to add. It is perfectly true that Śâkya does not receive the simple title of *Deva*. Why? Because that title is far too meager for such an exalted person, who is the *Devâtideva*, the paramount god of gods. He is called this in the *Lotus*, chapter 7, stanza 31 <note>1. Burnouf’s translation is 'Deva superior to the Devas.'</note>, and countless times throughout the whole range of Buddhist literature, in both Pâli and Sanskrit <note>2. The synonymous term *devâdhideva* is less frequent than *devâtideva*—for example, in the *Lalita-vistara*, page 131. The term *sarvadevottama*, meaning the highest of all gods, is essentially the same; see ibid., page 144.</note>. It is also undeniable that the title *Âdibuddha* does not appear in the *Lotus*, but it is suggested that Śâkya is identical to the *Âdibuddha* in these words: "From the very beginning (*âdita eva*), I have awakened, brought to maturity, and fully developed them (the innumerable Bodhisattvas) to be fit for their Bodhisattva position <note>3. See chapter 14, page 295.</note>." It is only by accommodation that he is called *Âdibuddha*; he is properly *anâdi*, meaning he has existed from eternity and has no beginning. The Buddha most solemnly declares (chapter 15) that he reached *Bodhi* an immense time ago—not, as people imagine, for the first time at Gayâ. From the entire way in which Śâkya speaks of his existence in former times, it is perfectly clear that the author intended to convey that the Lord had existed from eternity, or—what amounts to the same thing—from the very beginning, from time immemorial, and so on.

Śâkya has not only lived for an infinite number of eons in the past, but he is to live forever. Ordinary people imagine that he enters Nirvana, but in reality, he only makes a display of Nirvana out of consideration for the weakness of humanity. He, the

The Buddha is anthropomorphic, of course; what god is not? The *Lotus*, far from emphasizing unavoidable human traits, endeavors as much as possible to represent the Lord and his audience as superhuman beings. In chapter 14, there is a great pause—as in a drama—of no less than fifty intermediate kalpas, during which Sâkyamuni and all his hearers remain silent <note>5. One intermediate kalpa is, in the system, equal to 8 yugas. Since 4 yugas total 4,320,000 years, it follows that the pause lasted 432 million years. Esoterically, kalpa has certainly denoted a short interval of time, but even if we take the "intermediate kalpa" to mean, in reality, a period of time equal to a few hours, the pause would not refer to a historical event.</note>. A second pause of 1,000—or according to a variant reading, 100,000—years is held in chapter 20. Now, it is difficult to conceive that any author would willfully and ostentatiously mention such traits if he wished to impress the reader with the idea that the narrative refers to human beings.

<page-num>xxvii</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

*Saddharma-pundarîka* intends to represent *Sâkya* as the supreme being, as the god of gods, almighty and all-wise. But what are we to understand by the words ‘god’ and ‘god of gods?’ That is the question. To find the answer, let us recall the theosophical notions prevailing in ancient India at certain periods.

In general, it may be said that the Upanishads recognize two supreme beings, who in a mystical way are somehow identified; one is the great illuminator of the macrocosm, and is sometimes called the Sun, at other times Ether; the other, the enlightener of the microcosm, is Mind or Reason <note>1. See, for example, *Khândogya-upanishad* III, 18 and 19; compare *Bhagavad-gîtâ* XV, 12.</note>. As soon as the Sun ceased to be considered an animate being or to be represented as such, he might continue, for worship’s sake, *honoris causâ*, to be called the highest god; the deity that actually remained was Reason, poetically termed the inward light. This idea is expressed by *Nîlakantha* in his commentary on *Bhagavad-gîtâ* V, 14, in the following terms: *Prabhus kidâtmâ sûrya ivâsmadâdînâm prakasakah*, the Lord (is) the intelligent Self that like a sun is the illuminator of ourselves and others <note>2. Compare *Bhagavad-gîtâ* XIII, 33: "Just as the one sun illuminates this whole world, so does the owner of the field (the body) illuminate the whole field, O descendant of Bharata." The *kshetra* here is the body, the *kshetrin* is Mind, Reason, or *âtman*. Compare *Sankara* on *Khândogya-upanishad*, at the place cited.</note>. Now the same author, in his notes on *Bhagavad-gîtâ* VI, 30, distinctly states that our inward consciousness—or as he puts it, the *pratyagâtman*, the individual Self, otherwise called *gîva*—is *Nârâyana*, that is, the supreme being. At IX, 28, he paraphrases *Nârâyana* as *sarveshâm pratyagâtman*, the individual consciousness of all (sentient beings); at XII, 14, he identifies *Nârâyana* with *nirgunam brahma*. Just as here and there *Nârâyana* is represented as clad in all the glory and majesty of a sovereign, as the illuminator and vivifier of the world—in one word, as the sun—so we find *Sâkyamuni* invested with all the grandeur and all the resources of a ruler of nature. Philosophically, both *Nârâyana* and his counterpart *Sâkyamuni* are *purushottama*, *paramâtman*, the highest brahman, or Mind. <meta>catchword: Sâkyamuni</meta>

...is, esoterically, the very same <term>muni</term> (sage), the beholder of good and evil, the <term>punyapâpekshitâ</term> <term>muni</term> that is spoken of in <term>Manu VIII, 91</term>. It is acknowledged in <term>Bhagavad-gîtâ IX, 14</term> and the following verses that the supreme being may be conceived and respected in different ways according to the degree of intelligence of various creatures. Some pay their worship by leading a virtuous life, others through pious devotion, others through contemplation, others by professing a strictly monistic philosophy <note>1. The followers of the Upanishads, <term>Aupanishadas</term>, who say, "I am God," or as <term>Nîlakantha</term> puts it, "I myself am the Lord <term>Vâsudeva</term>."</note>, and others by acknowledging a personal god <note>2. The Lord in the <term>Saddharma-pundarîka</term> allows himself to be viewed in all these various aspects. Whether the Buddha theory—as we find it developed in the Sûtra, not in plain words but through indirect language and ambiguities—should be called atheistic or not, is a matter of relatively little importance about which opinions may differ. This much, however, can be asserted: the Lotus and the <term>Bhagavad-gîtâ</term> are, in this respect, exactly on the same level.

The conclusion reached is that the <term>Sâkyamuni</term> of the Lotus is an ideal, a personification, and not an actual person. Traits borrowed—or rather surviving—from an older cosmological mythology, and traces of ancient nature worship abound in both the Lotus and the <term>Bhagavad-gîtâ</term>. Yet in the highest sense of the word, <term>paramârthatas</term>, the Supreme Person (<term>Purushottama</term>) in both is the center of mental life. It is possible that the ancient teachers of the <term>Mahâyâna</term> believed that such an ideal once walked in the flesh here on earth, but the impression left by the spirit and the letter of the entire work does not support that assumption. In later times, fervent followers of the <term>Mahâyâna</term> truly held that belief, as we know from the example of the pious <term>Hiouen Thsang</term>, who was evidently as earnest in his belief that the Lord once walked upon the soil of India as he was convinced that <term>Mañgusrî</term>, <term>Maitreya</term>, and <term>Avalokitesvara</term> existed as living beings. The contents of the separate chapters into which the <term>Sûtra</term> is divided may be described, summarily, as follows:

1. Prologue.
2. Awakening of the Lord from his mystic trance; display of his transcendent skill, proved by the apparent trinity of vehicles, while in reality there is but one vehicle.
3. Prophecy of the Lord regarding the future destiny of <term>Sâriputra</term>, his eldest son. The second turning of the wheel of the law on that occasion, with an incidental commemoration of the first turning near Benares. Parable of the burning house, to illustrate the skill of the good father in saving his children from the burning pains of mundane existence.
4. Another parable, illustrating the skill of the wise father in leading a child that has gone astray and lost all self-respect back to a feeling of his innate nobility and to happiness.
5. Parable of the plants and the rain, to illustrate the impartiality and equal care of the Lord for all creatures <note>2. Compare *Bhagavad-gîtâ* IX, 29, where <term>Nârâyana</term> declares: 'I am equal toward all creatures; none is hateful to me, and none is beloved;' *samo 'ham sarvabhūteshu, na me dveshyo 'sti na priyah*.</note>. Parable of the blind man, to suggest that phenomena have only an apparent reality, and that the ultimate goal of all endeavors must be to reach omniscience, which in fact is identical with complete nescience.
6. Various predictions as proofs of the power of the <term>Sugata</term> to look into the future.
7. He has an equal knowledge of the remotest past; his remembrance of the turning of the wheel by the <term>Tathâgata Mahâbhiññâñânâbhibhû</term>. Edifying history of the sixteen sons of the said <term>Tathâgata</term>.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Sûtra's composition, moving from a summary of its chapters to a discussion on its intended interpretation, universal relevance, and authorship.</meta>

<page-num>xxxii</page-num>
<header>SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA.</header>

This summary, however meager, will be sufficient to show that there is no lack of variety in our <term>Sûtra</term>. We may, indeed, be satisfied that its compilers intended to give an exposition of the principal truths of their religion in general, and of the specific tenets of their own system¹ in particular—the whole arranged with such careful attention that the <term>Sûtra</term> allowed for both an exoteric and esoteric interpretation. It contains a revelation of the state of affairs in the present, as well as in the past and the future—a revelation derived from a virtually eternal source, so that the doctrine taught in it must be considered valid not only for a certain spiritual brotherhood or church, but for the human race at large. The highest authority to whom the doctrine is attributed is not a specific individual who lived for a short span of time somewhere in India, but the sublime being who has his constant abode on the <term>Gridhrakûta</term>—that is, the one who is called <term>Kûtastha</term> in the terminology of other Indian creeds.

As a general rule, it may be said that in anonymous works of ancient Indian literature, we must distinguish between the authority and the author. In the *Lotus*, following the invocation in some manuscripts, we find the following couplet:

> Vaipulyasûtrarâgam paramârthanayâvatâranirdesam |
> Saddharmapundarîkam sattvâya mahâpatham vakshye ||

That is: "I shall proclaim the king of the <term>Vaipulya-sûtras</term>, which teaches how one arrives at the right method of attaining the highest truth; the *<term>Saddharma-pundarîka</term>*, the great road leading to substantiality (existing in abstraction)." The person speaking here is not the <term>Buddha</term>, who is neither the author nor the writer of the work. Must we then attribute the couplet to one of the ancient copyists? <term>Burnouf</term>² decidedly thinks so, and his opinion is supported by the fact that the verses do not appear in all manuscripts. confess that I am not so sure of it. As the *<term>Sûtra</term>*, like other compositions of the kind, begins with the solemn "Thus have I heard, etc.," it is at least possible that the couplet belongs to the compiler. I am not aware that the scribes were in the habit of using such expressions as *vak* or synonymous terms instead of *likh* (to write); and as we find in the *<term>Mahâvastu</term>* similar future forms like *vakshye*—namely, *udîrayishyam* and *upavarnayishyâmi*¹—where they can hardly be attributed to the scribe, it is safer to leave the question of whether the opening couplet of the *Lotus* is the work of a compiler or of a copyist undecided. This is especially true because the parallel phrase *athâto—vyâkhyâsyâmah*, frequently found immediately after the invocation in non-Buddhist writings, must be held to refer to the author, authors, or compilers.

The *Lotus* being one of the standard works of the *<term>Mahâyâna</term>*, the study of it cannot but be useful for the right appreciation of that remarkable system. A reading of the book will convince the reader that a statement by Professor Wassiljew² can only be accepted with some restrictions, when this scholar—so profoundly versed in the history and development of Northern Buddhism—says that the <term>Buddha</term> of the *<term>Mahâyâna</term>* is "neither the creator nor the ruler of the world; he remains the same cold, indifferent egoist, absorbed in Nothingness." The *<term>Tathâgata</term>* of the *Lotus* is passionless, indeed, but that does not involve his being an egoist. In general, it may be said that the spirit of the *<term>Mahâyâna</term>* is more universal and its ideal less monastic than that of the *<term>Hînayâna</term>*. According to Professor Rhys Davids, we must not seek the superior vital power which enabled the Great Vehicle to outlive the earlier teaching in certain metaphysical subtleties, but in the idea of a desire to save all living creatures; "the idea," to quote his own words³, "as summarized in the theory of <term>Bodhisattvaship</term>, is the keynote of the later school, just as <term>Arhatship</term> is the keynote of

<page-num>xxxiv</page-num>

early Buddhism.' The <term>Mahâyâna</term> doctors said in effect: 'We grant you all you say about the bliss of attaining <term>Nirvâna</term> in this life¹. But it produces advantage only to yourselves; and according to your own theory there will be a necessity for Buddhas in the future just as much as there has been for Buddhas in the past. Greater, better, and nobler, then, than the attainment of <term>Arahatship</term> must be the attainment of <term>Bodhisattvaship</term> from a desire to save all living creatures in the ages that will come.' The teaching of the <term>Lotus</term>, however, is different, and comes to this: that every one should try to become a Buddha. It admits that from a practical point of view one may distinguish three means—so-called Vehicles, <term>yânas</term>—to attain the highest good (*summum bonum*), <term>Nirvâna</term>, although in a higher sense there is only one Vehicle. These means are, in plain language, piety, philosophy or rather Yogism, and striving for the enlightenment and welfare of our fellow creatures; these means are designated by the terms: the Vehicle of (obedient) hearers or disciples, of <term>Pratyekabuddhas</term>, and of <term>Bodhisattvas</term>. Higher than piety is true and self-acquired knowledge of the eternal laws; higher than knowledge is devoting oneself to the spiritual welfare of others². The higher unity embracing the three separate Vehicles is the <term>Buddha-vehicle</term>.

The title of <term>Bodhisattva</term> is not always used in the same sense. Apart from a broad distinction we can draw—

<page-num>XXXV</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

Between human and superhuman <term>Bodhisattvas</term>¹—the latter are not considered here—we sometimes find the word applied to those people who, in the passage of our <term>Sûtra</term> referred to, are called <term>Srâvakas</term> (hearers or learners). This appears to be the case at least in <term>Nepâl</term>, as we know from the following passage²:

> ‘The <term>Buddha</term> is the expert in the wisdom of <term>Buddhism</term> (<term>Bodhijnâna</term>), whose first duty, as long as he remains on earth, is to communicate his wisdom to those who are willing to receive it. These willing learners are the “<term>Bodhisattvas</term>,” so called because their hearts are inclined toward the wisdom of <term>Buddhism</term>, and “<term>Sanghas</term>,” because of their companionship with one another and with their <term>Buddha</term> or teacher in the <term>vihâras</term> or coenobitic <note>monastic</note> establishments. The <term>Bodhisattva</term> or <term>Sangha</term> continues to be such until he has overcome the very last grade of that vast and laborious ascent, through which he is taught that he can “scale the heavens” and pluck immortal wisdom from its resplendent source; once this achievement is performed, he becomes a <term>Buddha</term>, that is, an Omniscient Being.’

Here the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> are clearly distinguished from the coenobitic monks; they are similarly distinguished in the <term>*Lotus*</term>³, in which we find them also acting as learned or wise men (<term>Panditas</term>), and as preachers or ministers of religion. Wassiljew (cited above) remarks about the <term>Bodhisattva</term>—the earthly one, of course—that ‘from one perspective, he seems to be the substitute for the ancient <term>Bhikshu</term>;’ from which we should not assume that the mendicant monks, as such, ceased to exist, for that is clearly not the case, but rather that the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> were tasked with the office of preaching. They are people who deserve to be honored both by mendicant monks and lay devotees⁴, and they formed, it seems, a type of learned clergy. They should not be confused, however, with the modern <term>Vagra-Âkâryas</term> or married clergymen in <term>Nepâl</term>. There is reason to suppose that one of the

The honorific titles given to the preachers or interpreters of the law were "wise" or "learned man," <term>Pandita</term>, because the word is so often applied to them that it seems more like a title than a common epithet¹. <term>Târanâtha</term> recognizes <term>Pandita</term> as a title², and considers it to be the equivalent of the older <term>Mahâbhadanta</term>; he distinguishes "<term>Bodhisattvas</term>" from "common <term>Panditas</term>" and "<term>Arhats</term>." How does this agree with the data in the <term>Lotus</term>? As has been suggested in a previous note, the three Vehicles are imitations of three <term>Âsramas</term> or stages in the model life of an <term>Ârya</term>, primarily that of a <term>Brâhman</term>. The stages are those of a student, a hermit living in the forest, and a <term>Sannyâsin</term>, <term>Yati</term>, or <term>Mukta</term>, who has completely renounced the world. The second stage, that of a householder, obviously does not exist for those who devote themselves to a monastic life. Our <term>Sûtra</term> does not dictate that the three stages must be gone through by the same persons, any more than the <term>Bhagavad-gîtâ</term> in the place cited requires that one should pass through the stages of study, knowledge, and meditation before deciding upon complete renunciation (<term>tyâga</term>); what follows from the context is only this: that the Vehicle of <term>Bodhisattvas</term> (namely, those who strive for the well-being of all creatures) is superior to the two preceding Vehicles. Since the Vehicle of the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> is the loftiest of the three, they themselves must be considered as occupying the highest rank. Now <term>Târanâtha</term> places the <term>Arhats</term> above them, and among the Nepalese, the first class of the monastic order is also that of the <term>Arhat</term>³. The question is, how are we to judge the relationship between <term>Arhats</term> and <term>Bodhisattvas</term> in the <term>Lotus</term>? As far as I can see, the compiler⁴ of the <term>Sûtra</term> describes facts, or supposed facts, which he knew from oral or literary tradition as having occurred in the past, whereas the actual state of things in his own time and shortly before is represented as occurring in the future. His <term>Arhats</term> are sages of the past, canonized saints; his human <term>Bodhisattvas</term> are sages,

There are in the book many indications that the art of preaching was highly valued and well-developed, and it may be supposed that a greater proficiency in hermeneutics combined with superior mental activity has enabled the <term>Mahâyâna</term> to supplant its rival, the <term>Hînayâna</term>, and to extend its spiritual conquests from the snows of Siberia to the luxuriant islands of the Indian Archipelago.

After having touched upon such points in the text of the <term>Saddharma-pundarîka</term> as seemed to require more special notice, it is appropriate for me to say a few words about the translation and its resources. In the first place, I must declare that I cannot speak in too warm terms of the benefit I have derived from the French translation by the illustrious Burnouf. I have taken that work throughout for my model, without being able to reach its excellence. The significant discrepancies between our translations are partly due to my having followed other manuscripts, and partly to a different interpretation, especially of frequently corrupt and difficult <term>Gâthâs</term>. The basis of my translation has been an old palm-leaf manuscript belonging to Dr. D. Wright's collection in the University Library of Cambridge. The manuscript is dated Newar era 159 (A.D. 1039) and was written in the reign of King Kâmadeva (?), in the bright half of the month Vaisâkha, on a Thursday¹. It is one of the most ancient Sanskrit manuscripts existing in Europe, and therefore I thought it advisable to follow its readings as much as possible, except in passages that were clearly corrupt. A second manuscript, unfortunately incomplete, comes from the same collection. Its date is unknown since the latter part of the codex is lost, but from the form of the characters, it may be inferred that it is not much more recent than the other codex². The difference between the two is not very great; yet there can be no doubt that the second manuscript belongs to another family. The *varietas lectionis* <note>Latin for "variety of readings" or variant readings.</note> is strikingly similar in kind to what we find in the different texts of the *Vagrakkhedikâ*, edited by Professor Max Müller.

The first manuscript has much in common with the London codices, from which Burnouf derived numerous variant readings in the notes of his translation. It is further removed from the Paris manuscript that formed the basis of Burnouf's version, but not as far as the second

### KUMÂRAGÎVA’S TRANSLATION OF SADDHARMA-PUNDA-RÎKA III, STANZAS 1–22, RENDERED INTO FRENCH BY STANISLAS JULIEN.

I have heard the sound of this law;
I have obtained what I had not yet received;
In my heart, I have felt a great joy.
The nets of doubt have all disappeared.
In the past, I received the instructions of the Buddha;
I have not lost the Great Vehicle.
The sound (the voice) of the Buddha is heard very rarely.—
It can destroy the mental torments of all mortals.—
I have obtained the exhaustion (complete deliverance) of my faults.
Having heard it, I was delivered from sorrows and mental torments.
When I dwell in the mountains (or in) the valleys,
Or else at the foot of the forest trees,
Whether I am sitting or walking,
I think constantly of this matter.
Alas, I address severe reproaches to myself;
I say: why do I deceive myself?
We also are the sons of the Buddha;
We entered the law together, free from imperfections.
In the future, we will not be able
To explain this unsurpassed law (anuttaradharma).
The thirty-two gold-colored signs (marks that have the color of gold),
The ten powers, the means of deliverance,
Are found together within the single law,
And yet I could not obtain these things;
The eighty marks of beauty,
The eighteen unique laws (not common to all),
Merits and virtues of this kind—
I have lost them all.
When I was walking alone,
I saw the Buddha in the midst of the great multitude;
His name and reputation filled the ten directions;
He bestowed benefits upon all creatures.

I think to myself that I have lost this benefit;
I, because I have deceived myself.
Constantly, day and night,
Every time I think of this matter,
I wanted to ask the World-Honored One,
Praising and glorifying the bôdhisattvas.
That is why, day and night,
I maturely examine such a thing—
Free from imperfections and difficult to conceive—
Which brings the multitude to the terrace of Enlightenment (Bôdhimanda).
Originally, I was attached to perverse views (to heresy);
I was a master of Brahmatcharis.
The World-Honored One knew my heart;
He pulled me from heresy and spoke to me of Nirvâna.
I completely rid myself of perverse views (of heresy);
In the law of emptiness, I obtained testimonies and proofs (I obtained the proof that I understood the law of emptiness).
Then, I said to myself
That I had succeeded in reaching Nirvâna.
But now I realize
That it is not the true Nirvâna.
If, one day, I manage to become a Buddha
And am endowed with the thirty-two marks of beauty,
The Dêvas, the Yakchas,
The dragons, the spirits, etc.,
Will honor and venerate me.
At that time, I will be able to say
That I have obtained complete Nirvâna forever.
The Buddha, in the great assembly,
Told me that I was to become a Buddha.
When I heard the sound of this law,
My doubts and my regrets completely disappeared.
At first, when I heard what the Buddha said,
In the depths of my heart, I was filled with astonishment and doubts.
(I said to myself:) Could the demon have taken the form of the Buddha
To trouble my heart?
The Buddha, having employed all kinds of means,
Comparisons, words, and skillful discourses,
My heart became as calm as the sea.
When I heard him, the net of my doubts was torn apart;
The Buddha said that in past ages

Countless Buddhas, who have obtained Nirvana,
Rested in peace by means of skillful means;
And as they all had explained this law,
So too the present and future Buddhas,
Whose number is infinite,
By the aid of every kind of skillful means,
Had explained and developed such a law.
Now, World-Honored One,
Since you were born and left your family,
You have succeeded in turning the wheel of the law
And in explaining it through skillful means.
The World-Honored One has revealed the true path.
Mara did not do this thing <note>he did not take the form of the Buddha</note>;
Therefore, I know for certain
That Mara did not disguise himself as the Buddha <note>literally: did not make himself Buddha</note>.
Because of the web of doubts to which I had surrendered myself,
I had said to myself that it was something done by Mara <note>that is, that Mara had taken the form of the Buddha</note>.
But when I heard his voice—gentle and flexible,
Deep, distant, and extremely subtle—
Explaining the pure law,
My heart was greatly rejoiced.
My doubts have disappeared forever;
I dwell in peace within the true science.
Decidedly, I must become a Buddha.
I will be respected by the Devas;
I will turn the supreme wheel of the law;
I will instruct and convert the Bodhisattvas.

It extended across one million eight hundred thousand Buddha-fields in the eastern quarter, so that all those Buddha-fields appeared completely illuminated by its radiance, from the great Avîki hell up to the highest point of existence. And the beings in any of the six states² of existence became visible, all without exception. Similarly, the Lord Buddhas staying, living, and existing in those Buddha-fields became fully visible, and the law they preached could be heard in its entirety by all beings. And the monks, nuns, male and female lay devotees, Yogins and students of Yoga—both those who had attained the fruits (of the Paths of sanctification) and those who had not—also became visible. Buddha-fields who pursued the Bodhisattva course with ability, due to their earnest belief in numerous and various lessons and the fundamental ideas, they, too, all became visible. Then this thought arose in the mind of the Bodhisattva Mahâ-sattva Maitreya: Oh, what a great wonder the Tathâgata displays! What may be the cause, and what is the reason for the Lord producing such a great wonder as this? And such astonishing, marvelous, inconceivable, and powerful miracles now appear, even though the Lord is absorbed in meditation! Why, let me ask about this matter; who here would be able to explain it to me? He then thought: Here is Mañgusrî, the royal prince, who has performed his office under former *Ginas* and planted the roots of goodness while worshipping many Buddhas. This Mañgusrî, the royal prince, must have witnessed such signs of the former Tathâgatas—those Arhats, those perfectly enlightened Buddhas—before; in the past, he must have enjoyed the grand conversations on the law. Therefore, I will ask Mañgusrî, the royal prince, about this matter.

Then Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva, addressed Mañguśrî, the royal prince, in the following stanzas:

1. Why, Mañguśrî, does this ray sent out by the guide of men shine forth from between his brows—this single ray issuing from the circle of hair? And why is there this abundant rain of Mandârava flowers?

2. The gods, overjoyed, drop Mañgûshaka flowers and sandal powder, which are divine, fragrant, and delicious.

3. This earth is, on every side, filled with splendor, and all four classes of the assembly are filled with delight, while the whole field shakes in six different ways, frighteningly.

4. And that ray in the eastern quarter illuminates the whole of eighteen thousand Buddha-fields simultaneously, so that those fields appear gold-colored.

<sig>D 2</sig>

buddhas, all of them made this reflection: What may be the cause, what the reason for the Lord so extremely extolling the skillfulness of the <term>Tathâgatas</term>? Why does he praise it by saying, ‘Profound is the law discovered by me;’ and why does he praise it by saying, ‘It is difficult for all disciples and <term>Pratyekabuddhas</term> to understand it’? And the venerable <term>Sâriputra</term>, who sensed the doubt and uncertainty of the four classes of the audience and guessed their thoughts from what was passing in his own mind—he himself being in doubt about the law—then said to the Lord: What, O Lord, is the cause, what is the reason for the Lord so repeatedly and extremely extolling the skillfulness, knowledge, and preaching of the <term>Tathâgata</term>? 58. When, splendidly marked with the thirty-two characteristics, I am illuminating this whole world, and, worshipped by many hundreds of beings, I show the unmistakable stamp of the nature of the law;

59. Then, *Sâriputra*, I think this: "How will all beings, by the thirty-two characteristics, recognize the self-born Seer, who of his own accord sheds his luster all over the world?"

60. And while I am thinking and pondering, when my wish has been fulfilled and my vow accomplished, I no longer <note>One manuscript reads *ka* ("and") for *na* ("not").</note> reveal Buddha-knowledge.

61. If, O son of *Sâri* <note>*Sârisuta*, otherwise *Sâriputra*. *Sârikâ* or *śârikâ* is the *Turdus Salica*, one of whose other names is *dûtî*, masculine *dûta*. 62. And considering them to be as they are, and seeing that they have not completed their duty in previous lives, I see how they are attached and devoted to sensual pleasures, infatuated by desire and blinded by delusion.

63. Driven by lust, they fall into distress; they are tormented in the six states of existence and fill the cemeteries <gloss>1</gloss> again and again; they are overwhelmed with misfortune because they possess little virtue.

64. They are continually entangled in the thickets of sectarian theories, such as, "It is and it is not; it is thus and it is not thus." In trying to reach a firm conclusion on what is found in the sixty-two (heretical) theories, they come to embrace falsehood and persist in it.

65. They are difficult to correct, proud, hypocritical, crooked, malicious, ignorant, and dull; therefore, they do not hear the good call of the Buddha, not even once in *kotis* of births.

66. To them, son of *Sâri*, I show a device and say: Put an end to your trouble. When I see beings tormented by misfortune, I lead them to see *Nirvâna*.

67. In this way, I reveal all those laws that are always holy and correct from the very beginning. And the son of Buddha who has completed his course shall one day be a *Gina*.

99. There has never been any being who, after hearing the law of those (leaders), will not become a Buddha <note>1</note>; for this is the fixed vow of the Tathâgatas: "By completing my own course of duty, let me lead others to enlightenment."

100. In future days, they will explain many thousands of *kotis* of topics of the law; in their Tathâgataship, they shall teach the law by revealing the single vehicle mentioned before.

101. The lineage of the law forms an unbroken continuity, and the nature of its properties is always apparent. Knowing this, the Buddhas—the highest among men—will reveal this single vehicle <note>2</note>.

102. They will reveal the stability of the law, its subjection to fixed rules, its unshakable permanence in the world, the awakening of the Buddhas on the high terrace of the earth, and their skillfulness.

103. In every direction of space stand Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, honored by gods and men; these also explain superior enlightenment for the well-being of all beings in the world.

104. While demonstrating their skillfulness, those Buddhas display various vehicles, though at the same time, they point toward the one single vehicle <note>3</note>: the supreme place of blessed rest.

## CHAPTER III.

### A PARABLE.

Then the venerable Sâriputra, pleased, glad, charmed, cheerful, and thrilled with delight and joy, stretched his joined hands towards the Lord. At that time, *Sâriputra*, the Buddha-field of that Lord, the *Tathâgata Padmaprabha*, which shall be called *Viraga*, will be level, pleasant, delightful, extremely beautiful to see, pure, prosperous, rich, quiet, abounding with food, and filled with many races of men¹; it will consist of lapis lazuli and contain a checkerboard of eight compartments distinguished by gold threads, each compartment having its jewel tree always and perpetually filled with blossoms and fruits of seven precious substances.

Now that *Tathâgata Padmaprabha*, etc., *Sâriputra*, will preach the law by means of three vehicles². Furthermore, *Sâriputra*, that *Tathâgata* will not appear during the decay of the *Aeon*, but will preach the law by virtue of a vow.

That *Aeon*, *Sâriputra*, will be named *Mahâratnapratimandita* (that is, "ornamented with magnificent jewels"). Do you know, *Sâriputra*, why that *Aeon* is named *Mahâratnapratimandita*? The *Bodhisattvas* of a Buddha-field, *Sâriputra*, are called *ratnas* (jewels), and at that time there will be many *Bodhisattvas* in that sphere called *Viraga*; they will be innumerable, incalculable, and beyond computation, even without counting those computed by the *Tathâgatas*. On that account, that *Aeon* is called *Mahâratnapratimandita*.

In a certain village, town, borough, province, kingdom, or capital, there was a certain householder, old, aged, decrepit, very advanced in years, rich, wealthy, opulent; he had a great house, high, spacious, built a long time ago and old, inhabited by some two, three, four, or five hundred living beings. ### III. A PARABLE.

73

fire, became afraid, frightened, and anxious in his mind, and made the following reflection: "I myself am able to come out from the burning house through the door, quickly and safely, without being touched or scorched by that great mass of fire; but my children, those young boys, are staying in the burning house, playing, amusing, and entertaining themselves with all sorts of sports. They do not perceive, nor know, nor understand, nor care that the house is on fire, and they do not become afraid. Though scorched by that great mass of fire, and affected by such a great deal of pain, they do not mind the pain, nor do they conceive the idea of escaping."

The man, *Sâriputra*, is strong and has powerful arms, and so he makes this reflection: "I am strong and have powerful arms; so, let me gather all my little boys and take them to my chest to bring about their escape from the house." A second reflection then presented itself to his mind: "This house has only one opening; the door is shut; and those boys, fickle, unsteady, and childlike as they are, will, it is feared, run here and there and come to grief and disaster in this mass of fire. Therefore, I will warn them." Having so resolved, he calls to the boys: "Come, my children; the house is burning with a mass of fire; come, lest you be burned in that mass of fire and come to grief and disaster." But the ignorant boys do not heed the words of him who is their well-wisher; they are not afraid, not alarmed, and feel no misgiving; they do not care, nor flee, nor even know or understand the meaning of the word 'burning'; on the contrary, they run here and there, walk about, and repeatedly look at their father; all because they are so ignorant.

One has no time to wait for the other, and they push each other along, crying, "Who shall arrive first, the very first?"

110. But you, <term>Sâriputra</term>, have good will, not to mention my other disciples here. They will walk in my faith, even though each cannot have his own individual knowledge.

111. But do not speak of this matter to haughty or conceited people, nor to <term>Yogins</term> who are not self-restrained; for those fools, always reveling in sensual pleasures, might in their blindness scorn the revealed law.

112. Now hear the terrible consequences when someone scorns my skillfulness and the Buddha-rules forever fixed in the world; when someone, with a sullen expression, scorns the vehicle.

113. Hear the destiny of those who have scorned a <term>Sûtra</term> such as this, whether during my lifetime or after my <term>Nirvâna</term>, or who have wronged the monks.

114. After disappearing from among men, they will dwell in the lowest hell (<term>Avîki</term>) for an entire <term>kalpa</term>, and afterward they will fall lower and lower—those fools—passing through repeated births for many intermediate <term>kalpas</term>.

115. And when they have vanished from among the inhabitants of hell, they will descend further to the state of animals, becoming like dogs and jackals, and will become a sport for others.

116. In those circumstances, they will grow dark in color, spotted, covered with sores, and itchy; furthermore, they will be hairless and feeble—all those who have an aversion to my supreme enlightenment.

117. They are always despised among animals; hit by clods of earth or weapons, they yell; they are threatened everywhere with sticks, and their bodies are emaciated from hunger and thirst.
118. Sometimes they become camels or asses, carrying heavy loads, and are beaten with whips¹ and sticks; they are constantly occupied with thoughts of eating—those fools who have scorned the Buddha-rule.
119. At other times they become ugly jackals, half-blind and crippled²; the helpless creatures are harassed by the village boys, who throw clods and weapons at them.
120. Again, departing from that place, those fools become animals with bodies five hundred <term>yoganas</term> long, whirling around, dull and lazy.
121. They have no feet and creep on their bellies³; to be devoured by many <term>kotis</term> of animals is the dreadful punishment they must suffer for having scorned a <term>Sûtra</term> like this.
122. And whenever they take a human form, they are born crippled, maimed⁴, crooked, one-eyed, blind, dull, and lowly, because they have no faith in my <term>Sûtra</term>.

<header>### SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA. III.</header>

123. No one takes their side¹; a foul smell continually issues from their mouths; an evil spirit has entered the bodies of those who do not believe in this supreme enlightenment.

124. Needy and forced to perform menial labor, they are always in another’s service; feeble and subject to many diseases, they wander the world unprotected.

125. The person whom they happen to serve is unwilling to give them much, and what he does give is soon lost. Such is the fruit of sinfulness.

126. Even the best-prepared medicines, administered to them by skilled men, only increase their illness under those circumstances, and the disease never ends.

127. Some commit thefts, brawls, assaults, or acts of hostility, while others steal goods; all of this befalls the sinner.

128. He who scorns my Buddha-rule never beholds the Lord of the world, the King of kings ruling the earth², for he is doomed to live at the wrong time³.

129. Nor does that foolish person listen to the law; he is deaf and senseless; he never finds rest because he has scorned this enlightenment.

130. During many hundreds of thousands of myriads of <term>kotis</term> of eons, equal to the sands of the Ganges, he shall be dull and defective; that is the evil result of scorning this <term>Sutra</term>.

131. Hell is his garden (or monastery), and a place of misfortune¹ is his home; he lives constantly among donkeys, hogs, jackals, and dogs.

132. And when he has taken a human form, he will be blind, deaf, and foolish, the servant of another, and always poor.

133. Diseases, myriads of <term>kotis</term> of wounds on the body, scabs, itching, skin-flakes, leprosy, blemishes, and a foul smell are his covering and clothing in that state.

134. His sight is too dim to distinguish what is real. His anger appears powerful within him, and his passion is most violent; he always finds pleasure in animal rebirths.

135. If I were to continue for a whole <term>eon</term>, <term>Sariputra</term>, listing the evils of one who scorns my <term>Sutra</term>, I would never reach the end.

136. And because I am fully aware of this, I command you, <term>Sariputra</term>, that you must not explain a <term>Sutra</term> like this to foolish people.

137. But to those who are sensible, educated, thoughtful, clever, and learned, and who strive for the highest supreme enlightenment—to them, explain its real meaning.

138. To those who have seen many <term>kotis</term> of <term>Buddhas</term>, planted immeasurably many roots of goodness, and taken a strong vow—to them, explain its real meaning.

139. To those who are full of energy and always kindhearted, who have for a long time been developing the feeling of kindness and have sacrificed body and life—in their presence, you may preach this <term>Sutra</term>.

->DISPOSITION.<-

As the venerable Subhûti, the venerable Mahâ-Kâtyâyana, the venerable Mahâ-Kâsyapa, and the venerable Mahâ-Maudgalyâyana heard this teaching, never heard before, and as they heard from the mouth of the Lord the future destiny of Sâriputra to supreme perfect enlightenment, they were struck with wonder, amazement, and rapture. They immediately rose from their seats and went up to the place where the Lord was sitting; after throwing their cloaks over one shoulder, fixing their right knees on the ground, and lifting up their joined hands before the Lord, looking up to him with their bodies bowed and inclined, they addressed the Lord in this way:

Lord, we are old, aged, and advanced in years; honored as seniors in this assembly of monks. Worn out by old age, we imagined that we had attained <term>Nirvâna</term>; we made no efforts, O Lord, for supreme perfect enlightenment; our strength and exertion are inadequate for it. Therefore, O Lord, we are unable, despite the Lord's preaching, to

We were oppressed, O Lord, by three difficulties: namely, the difficulty of pain, the difficulty of conceptions<sup>1</sup>, and the difficulty of transition (or evolution); and in the worldly whirl, we were inclined toward what is low<sup>2</sup>. Once directed to them, we have been practicing, making efforts, and seeking nothing but *Nirvâna* as our payment<sup>3</sup>. We were content, O Lord, with the *Nirvâna* we obtained, and we thought we had gained much from the Tathâgata because we had applied ourselves to these laws, practiced, and made efforts. But the Lord takes no notice of us, does not mingle with us, and does not tell us that this treasure of the Tathâgata's knowledge shall belong to us, even though the Lord skillfully appoints us as heirs to this treasure of the knowledge of the Tathâgata. And we, O Lord, are not (impatiently) longing to enjoy it, because we already consider it a great gain to receive *Nirvâna* from the Lord as our payment. We preach a sublime sermon about the knowledge of the Tathâgata to the Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas; we explain, show, and demonstrate the knowledge of the Tathâgata, O Lord, without longing for it ourselves. It is for this reason that the Lord just now tells us that we are to him as sons <note>And, the Lord's actual sons.</note>, and that he reminds us of being heirs to the Tathâgata. For the case stands thus: we are as sons <note>And, the Tathâgata's actual sons.</note> to the Tathâgata, but humble of disposition <note>Rather, position or status.</note>; the Lord perceives the strength of our disposition and applies to us the title of Bodhisattvas. We are, however, charged with a double office; while in the presence of Bodhisattvas we are called persons of low disposition, at the same time we must awaken them to Buddha-enlightenment. Knowing the strength of our disposition, the Lord has spoken thus. In this way, O Lord, we say that we have obtained unexpectedly and without longing the jewel of omniscience, which we did not desire, nor seek, nor search after, nor expect, nor require; and we have received it because we are the sons of the Tathâgata.

On that occasion, the venerable Mahâ-Kâsyapa uttered the following stanzas:

> 1. We are filled with wonder, amazement, and rapture at hearing a voice <note>Or call.</note>; it is the lovely voice, the leader's voice, that we hear so unexpectedly today.
> 2. In a short moment, we have acquired a great heap of precious jewels such as we were not thinking of, nor requiring. All of us are astonished to hear it.
> 3. It is like the story of a young <note>*Bâla*, the word used in the text, may mean young as well as ignorant and foolish. Burnouf translates *bâlaganena* as "by a group of children."</note> person who, led astray by foolish people, went away from his father and wandered to another far distant country.

<summary>Mahâ-Kâsyapa and the disciples express their amazement at being recognized as the Buddha's true heirs and receiving the gift of omniscience. They begin a poetic retelling of the parable of the son who wandered far from his father.</summary>
