## CHAPTER V.

### ON PLANTS.

Thereupon the Lord addressed the venerable <term>Mahâ-Kâsyapa</term> and the other senior great disciples, and said: "Very well, very well, Kâsyapa; you have done very well to proclaim the real qualities of the <term>Tathâgata</term>. These are the real qualities of the <term>Tathâgata</term>, Kâsyapa, but he has many more—innumerable and incalculable—the end of which it would be difficult to reach, even if one were to continue enumerating them for immeasurable Eons. The <term>Tathâgata</term>, Kâsyapa, is the master of the law, the king, lord, and master of all laws. And whatever law has been instituted by the <term>Tathâgata</term> for any case remains unchanged. All laws, Kâsyapa, have been appropriately instituted by the <term>Tathâgata</term>. In his <term>Tathâgata</term>-wisdom, he has instituted them in such a manner that all those laws finally lead to the stage of those who know all <note>'All-knowing' is one of the most frequent euphemistic phrases used to refer to the state of the dead. Thus, 'all-knowing' (<term>sarvagña</term>) and 'knowing nothing' (<term>agña</term>) essentially mean the same thing; therefore, the commentator on the <term>Bhâgavata-Purâna</term> X, 78, 6 could appropriately identify <term>agña</term> and <term>sarvagña</term>.</note>. The <term>Tathâgata</term> also distinctly knows the meaning of all laws. The <term>Tathâgata</term>, the <term>Arhat</term>, etc., possesses the faculty of penetrating all laws and the highest perfection of knowledge, so that he is able to decide all laws, display the knowledge of the all-knowing, and impart the knowledge of the all-knowing."

<summary>The Buddha praises Mahâ-Kâsyapa for describing the Tathâgata's qualities and explains that the Tathâgata is the supreme master of all laws, using his infinite wisdom to guide all beings toward ultimate knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Mahâ-Kâsyapa, Tathâgata, Buddhist law, Eons, Arhat, sarvagña, agña, Bhâgavata-Purâna, enlightenment, spiritual wisdom</keywords>

--- Page 165 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse of the Lord (the Buddha) to Kâsyapa, transitioning into the famous "Parable of the Rain Cloud" to illustrate how the one Dharma is received differently by various beings.</meta>

<page-num>119</page-num>
<header>V. ON PLANTS.</header>

and establish the knowledge of the all-knowing.

It is a situation, Kâsyapa, similar to that of a great cloud full of rain, rising up in this vast universe over all the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees of various species and kinds—families of plants with different names growing on the earth, on hills, or in mountain caves. This cloud covers the wide universe to pour down its rain everywhere at the same time. Then, Kâsyapa, the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and wild trees in this universe—those with young and tender stalks, twigs, leaves, and foliage; those with middle-sized stalks, twigs, leaves, and foliage; and those that are fully developed—all these grasses, shrubs, herbs, and wild trees, both smaller and larger trees, will each, according to its own capacity and power, absorb the moisture from the water released by that great cloud. Through that water, which is all of one essence and has been abundantly poured down by the cloud, each plant will, according to its own seed, achieve regular development, growth, sprouting, and size. In this way, they will produce blossoms and fruits, and each will receive its own name. Although rooted in one and the same soil, all those families of plants and seeds are drenched and brought to life by water that is of one essence throughout.

In the same way, Kâsyapa, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, the <term>Arhat</term>, etc., appears in the world. Like a great cloud rising, the <term>Tathâgata</term> appears and sends out his call to the entire world, including gods, men, and demons <note>Parganya or Indra, *Jupiter pluvius*, is at the same time the thunderer, *Jupiter tonans*.</note>. And just as a

<summary>The Buddha introduces the Parable of the Rain Cloud, explaining how a single rainfall nourishes diverse plants differently according to their individual nature. Similarly, the Tathâgata appears in the world to provide a universal teaching that beings absorb according to their own capacities.</summary>
<keywords>Parable of the Rain Cloud, Kâsyapa, Tathâgata, Arhat, Indra, Parganya, spiritual growth, Dharma, universal teaching</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Parable of the Rain Cloud," where the Buddha explains his role as a universal teacher who provides the same Dharma to all beings, just as a single cloud rains upon all plants equally.</meta>

<page-num>120</page-num>
<header>SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA. V.</header>

...great cloud, Kâsyapa, extending over the whole universe, in like manner, Kâsyapa, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, the <term>Arhat</term>, etc., before the face of the world, including gods, men, and demons, lifts his voice and utters these words: I am the <term>Tathâgata</term>, O you gods and men! the <term>Arhat</term>, the perfectly enlightened one; having reached the shore myself, I carry others to the shore; being free, I set others free; being comforted, I comfort others; being perfectly at rest, I lead others to rest. By my perfect wisdom, I know both this world and the next, exactly as they really are. I am all-knowing and all-seeing. Come to me, you gods and men! Hear the law. I am the one who indicates the path; who shows the path, as one who knows the path and is acquainted with the path. Then, Kâsyapa, many hundred thousand myriads of <term>ko*t*is</term> of beings come to hear the law of the <term>Tathâgata</term>; and the <term>Tathâgata</term>, who knows the differences in the faculties and the energy of those beings, produces various <term>Dharmaparyâyas</term>, tells many tales—amusing, agreeable, both instructive and pleasant—tales by means of which all beings not only become pleased with the law in this present life, but also after death will reach happy states, where they will enjoy many pleasures and hear the law. By listening to the law, they will be freed from hindrances and in due course apply themselves to the law of the all-knowing, according to their own faculty, power, and strength.

Even as the great cloud, Kâsyapa, after expanding over the whole universe, pours out the same water and refreshes all grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees; even as all these grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees, according to their faculty, power, and strength, absorb the water and thereby attain full development...

<summary>The Buddha compares himself to a great rain cloud that provides the same teaching to all beings, allowing them to grow and reach enlightenment according to their individual capacities. He identifies himself as an all-knowing guide who leads others to the "shore" of liberation and peace.</summary>

The horizon shrouds all space in darkness and covers the earth.

6. That great rain cloud, heavy with water, is wreathed with flashes of lightning and rouses all creatures with its thundering call.

7. By blocking the sunbeams, it cools the region; and gradually lowering until it is within reach, it begins pouring down its water all around.

8. And so, flashing on every side, it pours out an abundant mass of water equally and refreshes this earth.

9. And all plants which have sprung up on the face of the earth—all grasses, shrubs, forest trees, and other trees, both small and great;

10. The various fruits of the field and whatever is green; all plants on hills, in caves, and in thickets;

11. All those grasses, shrubs, and trees are given life by the cloud that both refreshes the thirsty earth and waters the plants.

12. Grasses and shrubs absorb the water of one essence which issues from the cloud, each according to its own capacity and reach.

13. And all trees—great, small, and lowly—drink that water according to their growth and capacity, and grow vigorously.

14. The great plants, whose trunks, stalks, bark, twigs, pith, and leaves are moistened by the water from the cloud, develop their blossoms and fruits.

15. They yield their products, each according to its own capacity, reach, and the particular nature of the seed; yet the water released from the cloud is of only one essence.

Mahâ-Kâsyapa said to him: "Lord, if there are not three vehicles, for what reason then is the designation of disciples (*Srâvakas*), Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas maintained in the present times?"

In response to this speech, the Lord answered the venerable Mahâ-Kâsyapa as follows: "It is, Kâsyapa, as if a potter made different vessels out of the same clay. Some of those pots are to contain sugar, others ghee, others curds and milk; others, of inferior quality, are vessels for impurities. There is no difference in the clay used; no, the diversity of the pots is only due to the substances which are put into each of them. In the same way, Kâsyapa, there is only one vehicle, namely the Buddha-vehicle; there is no second vehicle, no third."

The Lord having thus spoken, the venerable Mahâ-Kâsyapa said: "Lord, if beings have different dispositions, will there be for those who have left the triple world one Nirvâna, or two, or three?" The Lord replied: "Nirvâna, Kâsyapa, is a consequence of understanding that all laws (things) are equal. Hence there is only one *Nirvâna*, not two, not three. <note>Compare Ecclesiastes 9:2: ‘All things come alike to all: there is one event for the righteous and for the wicked; for the good and for the clean, and for the unclean.’</note> Therefore, Kâsyapa, I will tell you a parable, for people of good understanding will generally easily enough grasp the meaning of what is taught in the form of a parable.

## CHAPTER VI.

### ANNOUNCEMENT OF FUTURE DESTINY.

After pronouncing these stanzas, the Lord addressed the full assembly of monks: "I announce to you, monks, I make known to you that the monk <term>Kâsyapa</term>, my disciple who is present here, shall pay homage to thirty thousand <term>koṭis</term> of Buddhas. He shall respect, honor, and worship them, and he shall keep the true law of those Lords and Buddhas. In his last bodily existence¹ in the world <term>Avabhâsa</term> (meaning luster), in the age (<term>aeon</term>) <term>Mahâvyûha</term> (meaning great division), he shall be a <term>Tathâgata</term>, an <term>Arhat</term>, and so forth, by the name of <term>Raśmiprabhâsa</term> (meaning beaming with rays). His lifetime shall last twelve intermediate <term>kalpas</term>, and his true law twenty intermediate <term>kalpas</term>; the imitation of his true law shall last for the same number of intermediate <term>kalpas</term>. His <term>Buddha-field</term> will be pure, clean, and free of stones, grit, and gravel; free of pits and precipices; free of gutters and dirty pools²; even, lovely, beautiful, and pleasant to see. It will consist of <term>lapis lazuli</term>, be adorned with jewel-trees, and look like a checkerboard with eight compartments marked with gold threads. It will be strewn

## CHAPTER VII.

### ANCIENT DEVOTION <note>1 Pūrvayoga, which recurs as the heading of chapters 22 and 25, would at first sight seem to mean 'former conjunction,' but that does not fit any better than 'ancient devotion.' I think that *yoga* here is an alteration of *yuga* (age, period), or a Prakritism for *yauga*, meaning something referring to an age. A Sanskrit *pūrva-yauga* would be formed like *pūrva-yāyāta*, etc.; compare Pāṇini VI, 2, 103. The original meaning of *pūrva-yoga* is, I suppose, pre-history. Compare *pubbayogo ti pubbakammam*, Milinda Pañho, p. 2.</note>.

Long ago, monks, in the past—incalculable, more than incalculable, inconceivable, immense, measureless eons ago, indeed, at a period, an epoch far beyond—there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, etc., named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, endowed with knowledge and conduct <note>2 That is, with light and motion.</note>, a Sugata, etc., etc., in the sphere Sambhava (that is, origin, genesis), in the period Mahārūpa. (You ask), monks, how long ago was it since that Tathāgata was born? Well, suppose some man were to reduce the entire mass of the earth element to powder, as much as is to be found in this whole universe; and after taking one atom of dust from this world, he were to walk a thousand worlds farther in an easterly direction to deposit that single atom; and after taking a second atom of dust and walking a thousand worlds farther, he deposits that second atom; and proceeding in this way, he at last gets the whole of the earth element deposited in the eastern

direction. Now, monks, what do you think of it? Is it possible by calculation to find the end or limit of these worlds? They answered: "Certainly not, Lord; certainly not, Sugata." The Lord said: "On the contrary, monks, some arithmetician or master of arithmetic might, indeed, be able by calculation to find the end or limit of the worlds, both those where the atoms have been deposited and where they have not; but it is impossible by applying the rules of arithmetic to find the limit of those hundred thousands of myriads of eons. So long, so inconceivable, so immense is the number of eons which have elapsed since the passing of that Lord, the Tathāgata Abhigñājñānābhibhū. Yet, monks, I perfectly remember that Tathāgata who has been extinct for so long a time <note>1 Hence it follows that the Buddha has existed since time immemorial; in other words, that he is Ādibuddha.</note>, as if he had reached extinction today or yesterday <note>2 I have taken the liberty to translate *svas* as 'yesterday,' though I have no other warrant for the word ever being taken in this sense except the context and the fact that in various languages the notions of tomorrow and yesterday are occasionally expressed by the same term, e.g., Hindi *kal* (properly morning, tomorrow, Sanskrit kalyam, *kālyam*); the English 'yesterday' is the very same word as the Gothic *gistradagis*, tomorrow.</note>, because I possess the mighty knowledge and sight of the Tathāgata."

is, O monks, no second vehicle at all in this world, no second Nirvana, and far less a third. It is a clever device of the Tathagata, monks, that upon seeing creatures¹ far advanced on the path of destruction, who delight in the lowly and are plunged in the mud of sensual desires, the Tathagata teaches them that Nirvana to which they are attached.

By way of example, monks, suppose there is a dense forest five hundred *yoganas* in extent that has been reached by a large company of men. They have a guide to lead them on their journey to the Isle of Jewels. This guide—being skilled, clever, wise, and well-acquainted with the difficult passages of the forest—is to lead the entire company² out of the forest. Meanwhile, that large troop of men—tired, weary, afraid, and anxious—say: “Truly, Master, guide, and leader, know that we are tired, weary, afraid, and anxious; let us return; this dense forest stretches so far.” The guide, who is a man of clever devices, seeing those people desiring to return, thinks to himself: “It should not be that these poor creatures fail to reach that great Isle of Jewels.” Therefore, out of pity for them, he uses an artifice. In the middle of that forest, he produces a magic city more than one or two hundred *yoganas* in extent. Thereafter, he says to those men: “Do not be afraid, sirs; do not return. There you see a populated place where you may rest and do all you have to do; stay there and enjoy a happy rest³. Let him who after

## CHAPTER VIII.

### ANNOUNCEMENT OF THE FUTURE DESTINY OF THE FIVE HUNDRED MONKS.

On hearing from the Lord that display of skillfulness and the instruction by means of mysterious speech; on hearing the announcement of the future destiny of the great Disciples, as well as the previous story concerning ancient devotion and the leadership<note>Vrishabhitva, a curious and irregular form instead of vrishabhatva.</note> of the Lord, the venerable Pûrṇa, son of Maitrâyanî, was filled with wonder and amazement, filled<note>Sphuṭa, in the sense of vyâpta; Pâli phuṭa.</note> with pure-heartedness<note>Nirâmishaḳittena. Nirâmisha is both ‘free from worldly taint and sensual desire,’ and ‘without having a lure or not eager for reward,’ i.e. disinterested. Both meanings are so intimately connected that it is not always easy to decide which we should prefer, e.g. Lalita-vistara, p. 215, and Manu VI, 49.</note>, and a feeling of delight and joy. He rose from his seat, full of delight and joy, full of great respect for the law, and while prostrating himself at the Lord’s feet, made within himself the following reflection: Wonderful, O Lord; wonderful, O Sugata; it is an extremely difficult thing that the Tathâgatas, etc., perform—conforming to this world, which is composed of so many elements, and preaching the law to all creatures with many proofs of their skillfulness, and skillfully releasing them when they are attached to one thing or another. And the Lord, observing the mental disposition of the venerable Pûrna, son of Maitrâyanî, addressed the entire assembly of monks in this manner: "You monks, see<note>Pasyata, variant reading: pasyadhvam.</note> this disciple, Pûrna, son of Maitrâyanî, whom I have designated as the foremost of preachers in this assembly, praised for his many virtues, and who has applied himself in various ways to understand the true law. He is the man to excite, arouse, and stimulate the four classes of the audience; tireless in the preaching of the law; as capable of preaching the law as he is of supporting his fellow followers on the path of duty. Except for the Tathâgata, monks, no one is able to equal Pûrna, son of Maitrâyanî, either in his essence or in his accomplishments. Now, monks, do you suppose that he maintains my true law alone? No, monks, you must not think so. For I remember, monks, that in the past, during the times of the ninety-nine Buddhas, this same Pûrna maintained the true law under the guidance of those Buddhas. We imagined, O Lord, that at the stage of <term>Arhat</term> we had reached <term>Nirvâna</term>. We live in hardship, O Lord, because we content ourselves with such a small degree of knowledge. In this you should see an effective method of mine, where from the expressions I used in preaching the law, you imagine <term>Nirvâna</term> to take place at this moment.<note>Or, at present, *etarhi*.</note>" And after having taught us the truth in such a way, the Lord now predicts our future destiny to supreme and perfect knowledge.

And on that occasion, the five hundred self-controlled <term>Arhats</term>, <term>Âgnâta-Kaundinya</term> and the rest, uttered the following stanzas:

> 34. We are rejoicing and delighted to hear this unsurpassed word of comfort—that we are destined for the highest, supreme enlightenment. Homage be to you, O Lord of unlimited sight!

> 35. We confess our fault before you; we were so childish, unlearned, and ignorant that we were fully content with a small part of <term>Nirvâna</term>, under the mastership of the <term>Sugata</term>.

<header>VIII. DESTINY OF THE FIVE HUNDRED MONKS.</header>

36. This is like the case of a certain man who enters the house of a friend, and that friend, being rich and wealthy, gives him much food, both hard and soft.

37. After satisfying him with nourishment, he gives him a jewel of great value. He ties it with a knot inside the upper robe and feels satisfied at having given that jewel.

38. The other man, unaware of it, goes out and travels from that place to another town. There he is met with misfortune and, as a miserable beggar, seeks his food in suffering.

39. He is content with the pittance he gets by begging, without caring for fine food; as for that jewel, he has forgotten it; he has not the slightest memory of it being tied in his upper robe.

40. In these circumstances, he is seen by his old friend who gave him that jewel at home. This friend properly reprimands him and shows him the jewel within his robe.

41. At this sight, the man feels extremely happy. The value of the jewel is such that he becomes a very rich man of great power, in possession of everything the five senses can enjoy.

42. In the same manner, O Lord, we were unaware of our former aspiration<note>¹ *Pranidhâna*; from the context one might understand that the real meaning was ‘predestination.’</note>, which was placed in us by the <term>Tathâgata</term> himself in previous existences from time immemorial.

43. And we were living in this world, O Lord, with dull understanding and in ignorance, under the

# CHAPTER IX.

## ANNOUNCEMENT OF THE FUTURE DESTINY OF ÂNANDA, RÂHULA, AND THE TWO THOUSAND MONKS.

On that occasion, the venerable Ânanda had this thought: "Will we also receive a similar prediction?" Thinking, pondering, and wishing this, he rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Lord’s feet, and spoke the following words. And the venerable Râhula also, in whom the same thought and the same wish arose as in Ânanda, prostrated himself at the Lord’s feet and spoke these words: "Let it be our turn as well, O Lord; let it be our turn as well, O Sugata. The Lord is our father and procreator, our refuge and protection. For in this world, including men, gods, and demons, O Lord, we are specially honored¹, as people say: 'These are the Lord’s sons, the Lord’s attendants; these are the keepers of the Lord's law-treasure.' Therefore, Lord, it would seem appropriate², if the Lord were soon to predict our destiny to supreme and perfect enlightenment."

Two thousand other monks and more, both those who were still in training and those who were not, likewise rose from their seats, placed their upper robes over one shoulder, and stretched out their joined hands

# CHAPTER X.

## THE PREACHER.

The Lord then addressed the eighty thousand Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas by turning to Bhaishagyarâga as their representative. "Do you see, Bhaishagyarâga, in this assembly the many gods, Nâgas, goblins, Gandharvas, demons, Garudas, Kinnaras, great serpents, men, and beings not human, monks, nuns, male and female lay devotees, followers of the vehicle of disciples, followers of the vehicle of Pratyekabuddhas, and those of the vehicle of Bodhisattvas, who have heard this Dharmaparyâya from the mouth of the Tathâgata?"

"I do, Lord; I do, Sugata."

The Lord proceeded: "Well, Bhaishagyarâga, all those Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas who in this assembly have heard even a single stanza, a single verse (or word), or who even by a single rising thought have joyfully accepted this Sûtra—to all of them, Bhaishagyarâga, among the four classes of my audience, I predict their destiny to supreme and perfect enlightenment. And whoever, Bhaishagyarâga, after the complete extinction of the Tathâgata, will hear this Dharmaparyâya and, after hearing it, if they joyfully accept even a single stanza, even with a single rising thought—to those also, Bhaishagyarâga, whether they are young men or young ladies of good family, I predict their destiny to supreme and perfect enlightenment. ### X.   THE PREACHER.   221

Those who hear this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> and then accept, penetrate, understand, and comprehend it are at that time near supreme, perfect enlightenment—so to speak, immediately close to it.

It is similar, <term>Bhaishagyarâga</term>, to the case of a certain man who, in need and in search of water, has a well dug in a dry stretch of land to obtain water. As long as he sees that the sand being dug out is dry and white, he thinks: "The water is still far off." After some time, he sees that the sand being dug out is moist, mixed with water, and muddy with trickling drops, and that the workmen who are engaged in digging the well are splattered with mire and mud. Upon seeing that sign, <term>Bhaishagyarâga</term>, the man will be convinced and certain that water is near. In the same way, <term>Bhaishagyarâga</term>, these <term>Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas</term> will be far away from supreme and perfect enlightenment as long as they do not hear, grasp, penetrate, fathom, or contemplate this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>. 

But when the <term>Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas</term> hear, grasp, penetrate, study, and contemplate this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>, then, <term>Bhaishagyarâga</term>, they will be, so to speak, immediately near supreme, perfect enlightenment. From this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>, <term>Bhaishagyarâga</term>, supreme and perfect enlightenment will come to all creatures. For this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> contains an explanation of the highest mystery, the secret article <note>¹ Or point.</note> of the law which the <term>Tathâgatas</term>, etc., have revealed for the perfecting of the <term>Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas</term>. Any <term>Bodhisattva</term>, <term>Bhaishagyarâga</term>, who is startled, feels anxiety, or becomes frightened by this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>,

He emphasizes that this discourse contains the highest secrets of the law revealed by the Buddhas for the perfection of all beings.</summary>

32. While he is living alone in the wilderness, I will send many gods and spirits to keep him company.

33. Such are the advantages he is to enjoy; whether he is preaching to the four classes or living as a solitary in mountain caves and studying his lesson, he will see me.

34. His fluency of speech knows no obstacle; he understands the many requirements of interpretation; he satisfies thousands of *kotis* of beings because he is, so to speak, inspired (or blessed) by the Buddha ³.

# CHAPTER XI.

## APPARITION OF A STÛPA.

Then a Stûpa, made of seven precious substances, arose from the ground in front of the Lord, with the assembly in the middle ^1. This Stûpa was five hundred <term>yoganas</term> in height and proportionate in circumference. After rising, the Stûpa—a meteoric phenomenon ^2—stood sparkling in the sky; it was beautiful and elegantly decorated with five thousand ^3 successive terraces of flowers ^4, adorned with many thousands of arches, and embellished by thousands of banners and triumphal streamers. It was hung with thousands of jewel-garlands, as well as with hour-plates and bells, and it emitted the scent of Xanthochymus and sandal, which filled this entire world. Its row of umbrellas rose so high as to touch the abodes of the four guardians of the

Then the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva Mahâpratibhâna, perceiving that the world—including gods, men, and demons—was filled with curiosity, said to the Lord: "O Lord, what is the cause, what is the reason for so magnificent a Stûpa of precious substances appearing in the world? Who is it, O Lord, who causes that sound to come out from the magnificent Stûpa of precious substances?" Having been asked this, the Lord spoke to Mahâpratibhâna, the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva, as follows: "In this great Stûpa of precious substances, Mahâpratibhâna, the physical body³ of the Tathâgata is contained in a condensed form; the Stûpa is his; it is he who causes this sound to go out."

The *Stûpa*, in the center of which the sun and moon sit together at that period, cannot be the rainbow, so we must again take *Stûpa* in the sense of *dhishnya*, or asterism; see note 1, p. 227. <header>SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA. XI.</header>

In those days, human life lasted a long time, so for a period of many hundreds of thousands of years, I exercised the rule of a King of the Law for the sake of duty, and not for the sake of pleasure¹. After installing the eldest royal prince in the government, I went in search of the best law in all four directions and had the following proclamation announced by the sound of a bell: "To whoever obtains the best law² for me or points out what is useful, I will become a servant." At that time, there lived a Seer; he told me: "Noble king, there is a Sûtra called the Lotus of the True Law, which is an exposition of the best law. If you consent to become my servant, I will teach you that law." And I, glad, content, exulting, and delighted by the words I heard from the Seer, became his pupil³, and said: "I will perform the work of a servant for you." And so, having agreed to become the servant of the Seer, I performed the duties of a servant, such as fetching grass, fuel, water, bulbs, roots, fruit, and so on. I also held the position of a doorkeeper. When I had done such work during the day, at night I tended to his feet while he

11. They will speak evil of us and spread the *Tirtha* doctrine². We will endure all that out of reverence for the great Seers.
12. And those fools who will not listen to us shall (sooner or later) become enlightened³, and therefore we will endure to the end.
13. In that dreadful, most terrible period of frightening general revolution, many fiendish monks will stand up as our critics.
14. Out of respect for the Chief of the world, we will bear it, however difficult it may be; girded with the belt of forbearance, I⁴ will proclaim this *Sutra*.
15. I⁵ do not care for my body or life, O Lord,

<note>² These passages are not very explicit, but this much is clear: the *Tirthikas* are somehow related to the Buddhists, yet distinguished from monks of other faiths who are entirely outside the Buddhist sects. # CHAPTER XIII.

## PEACEFUL LIFE.

Mañguśrî, the royal prince, said to the Lord: "Lord, what these Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas will attempt out of reverence for the Lord is difficult—most difficult. How are these Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas to proclaim this Dharmaparyâya at the end of time, in the final era?"

Then the Lord answered Mañguśrî, the royal prince: "A Bodhisattva Mahâsattva, Mañguśrî, who is to proclaim this Dharmaparyâya at the end of time, in the final era, must be firm in four things. In which things? The Bodhisattva Mahâsattva, Mañguśrî, must be firm in his conduct and his proper sphere if he wishes to teach this Dharmaparyâya.

And how, Mañguśrî, is a Bodhisattva Mahâsattva firm in his conduct and his proper sphere? When the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva, Mañguśrî, is patient and humble, and has reached the stage of humility; when he is not impulsive or envious; when, moreover, Mañguśrî, he clings to no law whatever and sees the true nature of the laws (or things); when he refrains from investigating and discussing these laws, Mañguśrî—that is called the conduct of a Bodhisattva Mahâsattva.

And what is the proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahâsattva, Mañguśrî? When the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva, Mañguśrî, does not serve, court, or attend to kings; does not serve, court, or attend to princes; when he does not approach them; when he does not

39. The wise man, the preacher, who wishes to expound this <term>Sûtra</term> must absolutely renounce falsehood, pride, slander, and envy.

40. He should never speak a disparaging word of anybody; never engage in a dispute on religious belief; never say to those who are guilty of shortcomings, "You will not obtain superior knowledge."

41. He is always sincere, mild, and patient; as a true son of <term>Sugata</term>, he will repeatedly preach the law without any feeling of frustration.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### ISSUING OF BODHISATTVAS FROM THE GAPS OF THE EARTH.

From the multitude of <term>Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas</term> who had gathered from other worlds, a number of <term>Bodhisattvas</term> equal to eight times the sands of the River <term>Ganges</term><note>The text reads *ashṭau Gaṅgânadîvâlikâsamâ Bodhisatvâs*. Burnouf translates the passage as "in a number equal to the sands of eight Ganges rivers." Perhaps "eight" should be understood as "eight thousand," just as in *Dîpavaṃsa* VI, 98, where the word eighty-four denotes eighty-four thousand.</note> then rose from the assembled circle. With their hands joined and stretched out toward the Lord to pay him homage, they said to him: "If the Lord will allow us, we would also, after the Lord's extinction, reveal this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> in this <term>Saha-world</term>; we would read, write, worship it, and wholly devote ourselves<note>Yogam âpadyemahi.</note> to that law. Therefore, O Lord, please grant us also this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>."

And the Lord answered: "No, young men of good family, why should you occupy yourselves with this task? ->SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA. XV.<-

By becoming increasingly convinced that the appearance of the Tathâgatas is precious (or rare), they will feel surprised and regretful, and while not seeing the Tathâgata, they will develop a longing to see him. The good roots developing from their earnest thoughts relating to the Tathâgata <note>That is, the virtuous intentions germinating in a person when they think about the shortness of life and the transitoriness of time.</note> will permanently lead to their well-being, benefit, and happiness. Such, young men of good family, is the Tathâgata's manner of teaching <note><term>Desanâparyâya</term></note>; when the Tathâgata speaks in this way, there is no falsehood on his part.

And the physician, seeing his sons afflicted with disease, overcome with pain and rolling on the ground, prepares a great remedy, having the required color, smell, and taste. He pounds it on a stone and gives it as a potion to his sons, with these words: "Take this great remedy, my sons, which has the required color, smell, and taste. For by taking this great remedy, my sons, you shall soon be rid of this poison or venom; you shall recover and be healthy." Those among the children of the physician who have correct perceptions, after seeing the color of the remedy, after smelling the aroma and tasting the flavor, quickly take it; as a consequence of this, they are soon totally delivered from their disease. But the sons who have distorted perceptions cheerfully greet their father and say: "Greetings, dear father, you have come back in safety and well-being; please heal us." They speak this way, but they do not take the offered remedy, and that because, owing to their distorted perceptions, that remedy does not please them in color, smell, or taste. 

Then the physician reflects: "These sons of mine must have developed distorted perceptions owing to this poison or venom, since they do not take the remedy nor heed me <note>One would rather have expected: joyfully accept my instructions.</note>. Therefore, I will use some skillful device to induce these sons to take this remedy." Prompted by this desire, he speaks to those sons as follows: "I am old, young men of good family, decrepit, and advanced in years; my term of life is near its end. But do not be sorry, young men—"

They are extremely sorry and mourn him deeply: "So then he is dead, our father and protector; he who fathered us; he, so full of bounty! Now we are left without a protector." Fully aware of being orphans and having no refuge, they are continually plunged in sorrow, through which their distorted notions give way to right notions. They recognize that the remedy possessing the required color, smell, and taste does indeed have the required color, smell, and taste, so they instantly take it, and by taking it are delivered from their illness. Then, knowing that these sons are delivered from illness, the physician shows himself again. Now, young men of good family, what is your opinion? Would anyone accuse^1 that physician of lying on account of his using that device? No, certainly not, Lord; certainly not, Sugata. He continued: In the same manner, young men of good family, I achieved supreme, perfect enlightenment an immense, incalculable number of hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Aeons ago, but from time to time I display such skillful devices to the creatures, with the view of educating them, without there being any falsehood on my part in that respect.

# XV. DURATION OF LIFE OF THE TATHÂGATA.

1. It has been an inconceivable number of thousands of kotis of Aeons—never to be measured—since I reached superior (or first) enlightenment and never ceased to teach the law.
2. I roused many Bodhisattvas and established them in Buddha-knowledge. I brought an endless myriad of kotis of beings to full ripeness over many kotis of Aeons.
3. I show the place of extinction; I reveal a device¹ to all beings to educate them, although I do not actually become extinct at the time, and I continue preaching the law in this very place.
4. There I rule myself as well as all beings². But people with perverted minds, in their delusion, do not see me standing there³.
5. Believing that my body is completely extinct, they pay worship to the relics in many ways, but they do not see me. They feel, however, a certain aspiration by which their minds become right⁴.
6. When such upright (or pious), mild, and gentle creatures leave their bodies, then I assemble the crowd of disciples and show myself here⁵ on the *Gridhrakûta*.
7. And then I speak to them in this very

16. But when mild and gentle beings are born in this world of men, they immediately see me revealing the law, because of their good works.

# CHAPTER XVI.

## OF PIETY.

While this explanation of the duration of the Tathâgata’s lifetime was being given, innumerable, countless creatures profited from it. Then the Lord addressed the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva Maitreya: "While this explanation of the duration of the Tathâgata’s lifetime was being given, Agita, sixty-eight hundred thousand myriads of *koṭis* of Bodhisattvas, comparable to the sands of the Ganges<note>1. *Ashṭashashṭînâm Gaṅgâ° Bodhisatvakoṭinayutasahasrâṇâm.* Burnouf connects *ashṭashashṭînâm* with *Gaṅgâ* and translates it as "sixty-eight Ganges." His version is justified by the similarity to other passages.</note>, have acquired the capacity to accept the law that has no origin. A thousand times more Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas have obtained *Dhâraṇî*<note>2. *Dhâraṇî* usually refers to a magic spell or a talisman. In some places, it is used interchangeably with *dhâraṇâ*, meaning support, remembering, or attention. The synonymous term *rakshâ* includes the meanings of both a talisman and protection or support. It is difficult to determine exactly what is intended in this text.</note>; and other Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas, equal to the dust atoms of one-third of a macrocosm, have by hearing this *Dharmaparyâya* obtained the faculty of unhampered view. # XVI. OF PIETY.

As soon as the Lord had given this explanation determining the duration and periods of the law, a great rain of Mandârava and large Mandârava flowers fell from the sky. These flowers covered and overwhelmed all the hundreds of thousands of millions of *kotis* of Buddhas who were seated on their thrones at the foot of the jewel trees across hundreds of thousands of millions of *kotis* of worlds. It also covered and overwhelmed the Lord Sâkyamuni, the Tathâgata, and so on, and the Lord Prabhûtaratna, the Tathâgata, and so on—the latter sitting fully extinct on his throne—as well as the entire host of Bodhisattvas and the four classes of the audience. A rain of heavenly powder made of sandalwood and agallochum trickled down from the sky, while higher up in the heavens, great drums resounded on their own with a pleasant, sweet, and deep sound. Hundreds and thousands of double pieces of fine heavenly cloth fell down from the sky. Necklaces, half-necklaces, pearl necklaces, gems, jewels, noble gems, and noble jewels were seen high in the air, hanging down from every side in all directions, while all around, thousands of jeweled incense burners, containing priceless and exquisite incense, moved of their own accord. Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas were seen holding rows of jeweled umbrellas high above each Tathâgata, reaching as high as the Brahma-world. Let us, on the other hand, suppose the case, Agita, that a young man or young lady of good family, on hearing this Dharmaparyâya containing the exposition of the duration of the Tathâgata’s life, conceives even a single thought of trust or believes in it; then that former accumulation of merit¹, that accumulation of good connected with the five perfections of virtue—that accumulation which has come to full accomplishment over eight hundred thousand myriads of *kotis* of Aeons—does not equal one-hundredth part of the accumulation of merit in the second case; it does not equal one-thousandth part; it admits of no calculation, no counting, no reckoning, no comparison, no approximation, and no secret teaching². Someone who possesses such an accumulation of merit, Agita, whether they are a young man or a young lady of good family, will not miss supreme, perfect enlightenment; no, that is not possible.

31. He who, renouncing doubt, vacillation, and misgiving, shall believe even for a short moment, shall obtain such a reward.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### AN INDICATION OF THE MERIT OF JOYFUL ACCEPTANCE.

After that, the <term>Bodhisattva Mahâsattva</term> <term>Maitreya</term> said to the <term>Lord</term>: "O <term>Lord</term>, if a person—whether a young man or a young lady of a good family—joyfully<note>Or, gratefully.</note> accepts this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> after hearing it preached, how much <term>merit</term>, O <term>Lord</term>, will be produced by such a young man or young lady?"

1. How great will be the merit of the one who, after the passing of the great Hero, hears this exalted <term>Sûtra</term> and joyfully accepts it?

...who produces merit by providing all beings in the four hundred thousand *Asaṅkhyeyas* of worlds with all the necessities for happiness and by establishing them in *Arhatship*; (consider) on the other hand the person who, being the fiftieth in the sequence of the oral tradition of the law, hears even a single stanza or a single word from this *Dharmaparyâya* and joyfully accepts it. If we compare the total merit connected with that joyful acceptance and the total merit connected with the generosity of that master of generosity, that great master of generosity, the greater merit will belong to the one who, being the fiftieth in the sequence of the oral tradition of the law, after hearing even a single stanza or a single word from this *Dharmaparyâya*, joyfully accepts it.

Against this accumulation of merit, Agita, this accumulation of roots of goodness connected with that joyful acceptance, the former accumulation of merit connected with the generosity of that master of generosity, that great master of generosity, and connected with the confirmation in *Arhatship*, does not equal a 1/100th part, nor a 1/100,000th, nor a 1/10,000,000th, nor a 1/1,000,000,000th, nor a 1/1,000 × 10,000,000th, nor a 1/100,000 × 10,000,000th, nor a 1/100,000 × 10,000 × 10,000,000th part; it allows for no calculation, no counting, no reckoning, no comparison, no approximation, and no secret teaching. So immense and incalculable, Agita, is the merit which a person, being the fiftieth in the sequence of the tradition of the law, produces by joyfully accepting even a single stanza or a single word from this *Dharmaparyâya*; how much more merit, then, will he produce, Agita, who hears this *Dharmaparyâya* in my presence and then joyfully accepts it? ## CHAPTER XIX.

### SADÂPARIBHÛTA.

The Lord then addressed the <term>Bodhisattva Mahâsattva Mahâsthâmaprâpta</term>. In a similar way, <term>Mahâsthâmaprâpta</term>, one may infer from what has been said that he who rejects such a <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> as this, who abuses monks, nuns, or male or female lay devotees keeping this <term>Sûtra</term>, or who insults them and treats them with false and harsh words, shall experience dire results to such an extent as is impossible to express in words. But those who keep, read, comprehend, teach, and extensively expound it to others shall experience happy results, such as I have already mentioned: they shall attain such a perfection of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as just described.

In the days of old, <term>Mahâsthâmaprâpta</term>, at a past period before incalculable <term>Aeons</term>—indeed, more than incalculable, immense, inconceivable, and even long before—there appeared in the world a <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., named <term>Bhîshmagargitasvararâga</term>, endowed with wisdom and conduct, a <term>Sugata</term>, etc. etc., in the <term>Aeon Vinirbhoga</term>, in the world <term>Mahâsambhava</term>. Now, <term>Mahâsthâmaprâpta</term>, that Lord <term>Bhîshmagargitasvararâga</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., in that world <term>Vinirbhoga</term>, showed the law in the presence of the world, including gods, men, and demons; the law containing the <term>four noble truths</term> and starting from the chain of causes and effects, tending to overcome birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and lamentation,

<summary>The Buddha warns Mahâsthâmaprâpta about the severe consequences of abusing those who follow the Lotus Sutra, while promising great physical and mental perfection to its devoted teachers. He begins a story of a past Buddha named Bhîshmagargitasvararâga who taught the four noble truths in a long-ago aeon.</summary>

# CHAPTER XX.

## CONCEPTION OF THE TRANSCENDENT POWER OF THE TATHÂGATAS.

Then, those hundreds of thousands of myriads of *kotis* of Bodhisattvas—as numerous as the atoms of dust in a universe—who had emerged from the gaps in the earth, all stretched their joined hands toward the Lord and said to him: "O Lord, after the complete passing of the Tathâgata, we will proclaim this *Dharmaparyâya* everywhere in all of the Lord's Buddha-fields, wherever the Lord shall have completely passed away¹."

"We are eager to receive this sublime *Dharmaparyâya*, O Lord, so that we may keep, read, publish, and write it."

At this sight, they felt struck with wonder, amazement, and rapture. And they heard a voice from the sky calling:

> Honorable ones, beyond a distance of an immense, incalculable number of hundreds of thousands of myriads of <term>kotis</term> of worlds, there is the world named <term>Saha</term>; there the <term>Tathâgata</term> called <term>Sâkyamuni</term>, the <term>Arhat</term>, etc., is just now revealing to the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <term>Mahâsattvas</term> the <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> of the <term>Lotus of the True Law</term>, a <term>Sûtrânta</term> of great extent, serving to instruct <term>Bodhisattvas</term>, and belonging specifically to all <term>Buddhas</term>. Accept it joyfully with all your heart, and do homage to the Lord <term>Sâkyamuni</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., and the Lord <term>Prabhûtaratna</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc.

On hearing such a voice from the sky, all those beings exclaimed from the place where they stood, with joined hands:

> Homage to the Lord <term>Sâkyamuni</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>.

Then they threw towards the <term>Saha-world</term> various flowers, incense, fragrant wreaths, ointment, gold, cloth, umbrellas, flags, banners, and triumphal streamers, as well as ornaments, finery, necklaces, gems, and jewels of all sorts, in order to worship the Lord <term>Sâkyamuni</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>¹, and this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> of the <term>Lotus of the True Law</term>. Those flowers, incense, etc., and those necklaces, etc., came down upon this <term>Saha-world</term>, where they formed a great canopy of flowers hanging in the sky above the <term>Tathâgatas</term> sitting there, as well as those in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of <term>kotis</term> of other worlds.

<header>XX. TRANSCENDENT POWER OF THE TATHÂGATAS.</header>

Then the Lord addressed the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <term>Mahâsattvas</term> led by <term>Viśishṭakâritra</term>: "Inconceivable, young men of good family, is the power of the <term>Tathâgatas</term>, and so on. In order to transmit this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>, young men of good family, I could continue for hundreds of thousands of myriads of <term>kotis</term> of <term>Aeons</term> explaining the manifold virtues of this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> through the different principles of the law, without reaching the end of those virtues. In this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>, I have briefly taught all <term>Buddha-laws</term> (or <term>Buddha-qualities</term>), all the superiority, all the mystery, and all the profound conditions of the <term>Buddhas</term>. Therefore, young men of good family, after the complete extinction of the <term>Tathâgata</term>, you should with reverence keep, read, proclaim, cherish,¹ and worship it. And wherever on earth, young men of good family, this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> is made known, read, written, meditated upon, expounded, studied, or collected into a volume—whether in a monastery or at home, in the wilderness or in a town, at the foot of a tree or in a palace, in a building or in a cavern—on that spot one should erect a shrine dedicated to the <term>Tathâgata</term>. For such a spot must be regarded as a terrace of enlightenment; such a spot must be regarded as one where all <term>Tathâgatas</term>, and so on, have arrived at supreme, perfect enlightenment; on that spot, all <term>Tathâgatas</term> have set in motion the wheel of the law; on that spot, one may consider that all <term>Tathâgatas</term> have reached complete extinction."

<header>SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA. XXI.</header>

# CHAPTER XXI.

## SPELLS.

Thereupon the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva *Bhaishagyarâga* rose from his seat. After placing his upper robe upon one shoulder and resting his right knee upon the ground, he lifted his joined hands to the Lord and said: "How great, O Lord, is the pious merit which will be produced by a young man or young lady of good family who keeps this *Dharmaparyâya* of the Lotus of the True Law, either in memory or in a book?"

Whereupon the Lord said to the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva *Bhaishagyarâga*: "Suppose, *Bhaishagyarâga*, that some man or young lady of good family honors, respects, reveres, and worships hundreds of thousands of myriads of *kotis* of Tathâgatas, equal to the sands of eighty Ganges rivers; do you think, *Bhaishagyarâga*, that such a young man or young lady of good family will on that account produce much pious merit?"

The Bodhisattva *Bhaishagyarâga* replied: "Yes, Lord; yes, Sugata."

The Lord said: "I announce to you, *Bhaishagyarâga*, I declare to you: any young man or young lady of good family, *Bhaishagyarâga*, who shall keep, read, comprehend, and in practice follow even a single stanza from this *Dharmaparyâya* of the Lotus of the True Law—that young man or young lady of good family, *Bhaishagyarâga*, will on that account produce far more pious merit."

Saddharma-pundarîka, Bodhisattva, Mahâsattva, Bhaishagyarâga, Dharmaparyâya, Lotus of the True Law, kotis, Tathâgatas, Sugata, pious merit.

<summary>In the opening of Chapter XXI, the Bodhisattva Bhaishagyarâga asks about the spiritual rewards for those who preserve the Lotus Sutra. The Buddha responds that even minimal devotion to a single stanza of the text generates greater merit than worshiping countless Buddhas.</summary>

Anyâ may be identified with the Vedic anyâ, inexhaustible, and synonymous with Aditi. Most of the other terms may be explained as synonymous with *pragñâ* (for example, *pratyavekshani*), with nature (*kshaye akshaye*), with the earth (*dhâranî*).</note>.

The Lord expressed his approval to the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva Bhaishagyarâga by saying: "Very well, Bhaishagyarâga; by these talismanic words being pronounced out of compassion for creatures, the common well-being of creatures is promoted; their guard, defense, and protection is secured."

Then the Bodhisattva Mahâsattva Pradânasûra said to the Lord: "I also, O Lord, will give talismanic words for the benefit of such preachers, so that no one seeking an opportunity to surprise such preachers may find that opportunity, whether it be a demon, giant, goblin, sorcerer, imp, or ghost; so that none of these, when seeking and spying for an opportunity to surprise, may find that opportunity." Thereupon the <term>Bodhisattva Mahâsattva</term> Nakshatrarâgasaṅkusumitâbhigña spoke to the Lord as follows: "Why, O Lord, does the <term>Bodhisattva</term> Bhaishagyarâga pursue his course<note>Pravikarati.</note> in this <term>Saha-world</term>, while he is fully aware of the many hundred thousands of myriads of <term>koṭis</term> of difficulties he has to meet? <header>XXII. ANCIENT DEVOTION OF BHAISHAGYARÂGA.</header>

<term>Sugata</term>, etc., etc. Now that <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., *Kandravimalasûryaprabhâsasrî* had a great assembly of eighty *kotis*<note>According to the Cambridge manuscript; Burnouf says eighty hundred thousand myriads of kotis.</note> of <term>Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas</term> and an assembly of disciples equal to the sands of seventy-two Ganges rivers. His spiritual rule was without women, and his <term>Buddha-field</term> had no hell, no animal kingdom, no ghosts, and no demons; it was level, neat, and smooth as the palm of a hand. <term>Sarvasattvapriyadarsana</term> applied himself to his difficult course. He wandered for twelve thousand years, strenuously engaged in contemplation. After those twelve thousand years had expired, he acquired the <term>Samâdhi</term> termed <term>Sarvarûpasandarsana</term> (that is, the sight or display of all forms). As soon as he had acquired that <term>Samâdhi</term>, being satisfied, glad, joyful, rejoicing, and delighted, he made the following reflection: "It is because of this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> of the Lotus of the True Law that I have acquired the <term>Samâdhi</term> of <term>Sarvarûpasandarsana</term>." Then he made another reflection: "Let me do homage to the Lord *Kandravimala-sûryaprabhâsasrî* and this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> of the Lotus of the True Law." As soon as he had entered into such a meditation, a great rain of <term>Mandârava</term> and great <term>Mandârava</term> flowers fell from the sky above. A cloud of <term>Kâlânusârin</term> sandalwood was formed, and a rain of <term>Uragasâra</term> sandalwood poured down. The nature of those essences was so noble that one *karsha* of it was worth the entire Saha-world.

After a while, <term>Nakshatrarâgasaṅkusumitâbhigña</term>, the <term>Bodhisattva Mahâsattva Sarvasattvapriyadarsana</term> rose from that meditation with memory and full consciousness, and reflected thus: "This display of magic power is not likely to honor the Lord and <term>Tathâgata</term> as much as the sacrifice of my own body will do." ## CHAPTER XXIII.

### GADGADASVARA.

At that moment, the Lord *Sâkyamuni*, the *Tathâgata*, etc., emitted a flash of light from the circle of hair between his eyebrows—one of the characteristic signs of a great man. By this flash of light, hundreds of thousands of myriads of *koṭis* of Buddha-fields, equal to the sands of eighteen Ganges rivers, were illuminated. Beyond those Buddha-fields, equal in number, is the world called *Vairokanaraśmipratimaṇḍita* (that is, embellished by the rays of the sun). There dwells, lives, and exists the *Tathâgata* named *Kamaladalavimalanakshatrarâgasaṅkusumitâbhigña*, who, surrounded and attended by a large and immense assembly of *Bodhisattvas*, preached the law. Immediately, the ray of light flashing from the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Lord *Sâkyamuni*, the *Tathâgata*, etc., filled the world *Vairokanaraśmipratimaṇḍita* with a great radiance. 

In that world *Vairokanaraśmipratimaṇḍita*, there was a *Bodhisattva Mahâsattva* called *Gadgadasvara*, who had planted roots of goodness, who had previously seen similar luminous flashes emitted by many *Tathâgatas*, etc., and who had acquired many *Samâdhis*, such as the *Samâdhi Dhvagâgrakeyûra* (that is, the bracelet at the upper end of the banner staff), *Saddharma-puṇḍarîka* (that is, the Lotus of the True Law), *Vimaladatta* (that is, given by Vimala), and *Nakshatrarâgavikrîḍita* (that is, the sport of the

# XXIV. THE ALL-SIDED ONE.

With such a faculty of transformation, young man of good family, the <term>Bodhisattva Mahâsattva Avalokitesvara</term> moves in this <term>Saha-world</term>.

And on that occasion the Lord uttered the following stanzas:

1. *Kitradhvaga* asked Akshayamati the following question: For what reason, son of *Gina*, is Avalokitesvara so called? <note>It should be observed that this poetic version differs entirely from the preceding prose introduction. Regarding the name *Kitradhvaga*, I have not encountered it elsewhere.</note>

2. And Akshayamati, that ocean of profound insight, after considering the situation <note>*Tâdrisatâ vilokiyâ*.</note>, spoke to *Kitradhvaga*: Listen to the conduct of Avalokitesvara.

3. Hear from my instruction how, for numerous, inconceivable Aeons, he has fulfilled his vow under many thousand *kotis* of Buddhas.

4. Hearing, seeing, and regularly and constantly thinking <note>The object (of whom or what) is not expressed. From what follows, one might be tempted to infer that Avalokitesvara, or the explanation of his power, is the object of hearing, etc.</note> will certainly destroy all suffering, mundane existence, and grief of living beings here on earth.

5. If one is thrown into a pit of fire by a wicked enemy with the intent of killing him, he has only to think of Avalokitesvara, and the fire shall be extinguished as if sprinkled with water.

6. If one happens to fall into the dreadful ocean, the home of <term>Nâgas</term>, marine monsters, and demons, he has only to think of Avalokitesvara, and he shall never sink down into the king of waters <note>Smarato (for smaratu), Avalokitesvaram galarâge na kadâki sîdati.</note>.

The verses emphasize that thinking of the Bodhisattva can save a person from fire, drowning, and worldly suffering.</summary>

Then the king *Subhavyûha* had the following thought: "The Buddha-knowledge must be very powerful, and the Tathâgata endowed with inconceivable good qualities, for this Tathâgata-image to manifest on the summit of the tower—an image so exquisite, beautiful, and possessing an extreme abundance of beautiful colors." # CHAPTER XXVI.

## ENCOURAGEMENT<note>Utsâhana (Encouragement).</note> OF SAMANTABHADRA.

Then the <term>Bodhisattva Mahâsattva Samantabhadra</term>, in the east, surrounded and followed by <term>Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas</term> beyond all calculation, amid the shaking of fields, a rain of lotuses, and the playing of hundreds of thousands of myriads of <term>kotis</term> of musical instruments, proceeded with the great splendor of a <term>Bodhisattva</term>, the great display of transformations appropriate to a <term>Bodhisattva</term>, the great magnificence of a <term>Bodhisattva</term>, the great power of a <term>Bodhisattva</term>, the great luster of a glorious <term>Bodhisattva</term>, the great majestic march of a <term>Bodhisattva</term>, the great miraculous display of a <term>Bodhisattva</term>, and a great visionary sight of gods, <term>Nâgas</term>, goblins, <term>Gandharvas</term>, demons, <term>Garudas</term>, <term>Kinnaras</term>, great serpents, men, and beings not human, who, produced by his magic, surrounded and followed him. <term>Samantabhadra</term>, then, the <term>Bodhisattva</term>, amid such inconceivable miracles worked by magic, arrived at this <term>Saha-world</term>. <note>1 In Burnouf’s translation we find the following added: *anuvarte vartani vartâli svâhâ*. All terms are, or ought to be, vocatives of feminine words in the singular. *Pati*, as in Pâli *pagâpati* and Buddhist Sanskrit *pragâpatî*, interchanges with the ending *vatî*; this occurs not only in *pragâvatî* (for example, in the *Lalita-vistara*), but also in some of the words occurring in the spell; for instance, instead of *dandapati*, the Tibetan text has *dandâvati*. As *Siva* in the *Mahâbhârata* XII, 10361 is represented as the personified *Danda*, we may hold that all the names above belong to *Siva’s* female counterpart, Durgâ. The epithet of *Simhavikrîditâ* is but a variation of Simhikâ, one of the names of Dâkshâyanî or Durgâ in her capacity as mother to Râhu. Compare the remarks on the spells in chapter XXI.</note>

The monks who, at the end of time, at the end of the period, in the second half of the millennium, keep this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>, will not be covetous, nor greedy for robes or vehicles<note>² <term>Yâna</term>; Burnouf read this as <term>pâna</term>, meaning drink. It is, indeed, generally impossible to distinguish between <term>pa</term> and <term>ya</term> in the Nepalese manuscripts.</note>. Those preachers will be honest and possess three forms of emancipation; they will refrain from worldly business. Those who lead monks who know this <term>Sûtrânta</term> into error will be born blind; and those who openly defame them will have a spotted body in this very world. Those who scoff and hoot at the monks who copy this <term>Sûtrânta</term> will have teeth that are broken and set far apart; they will have disgusting lips, a flat nose, contorted hands and feet, and squinting eyes; they will have a putrid body covered with stinking boils, eruptions, scabs, and itch. If one speaks an unkind word, whether true or not, to such writers, readers, and keepers of this <term>Sûtrânta</term>, it must be considered a very heinous sin. Therefore, <term>Samantabhadra</term>, people should, even from a distance, rise from their seats before the monks who keep this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> and show them the same reverence as they would to the <term>Tathâgata</term>.

While this chapter on the Encouragement of <term>Samantabhadra</term> was being explained, hundreds of thousands of <term>kotis</term> of <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <term>Mahasattvas</term>, as numerous as the sands of the river <term>Ganges</term>, acquired the talismanic spell <term>Avarta</term>.

<summary>The text concludes the warnings against disparaging the preachers of the Lotus Sutra, detailing the severe physical and karmic consequences for such actions, and notes that a vast number of Bodhisattvas achieved a special spell upon hearing this teaching.</summary>
<keywords>Samantabhadra, Mara, Dharmaparyaya, Sutranta, Tathagata, kotis, Bodhisattvas, Mahasattvas, Ganges, Avarta, karmic retribution, Buddhist law</keywords>

--- Page 486 ---
<meta>This page begins Chapter XXVII, the final chapter of the Lotus Sutra, marking the conclusion of the Buddha's discourse and the formal entrustment of the Dharma to his followers.</meta>

<page-num>440</page-num>
<header>SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA. XXVII.</header>

# CHAPTER XXVII.

## THE PERIOD¹.<note>¹ <term>Dharmaparyâya</term>, properly, the period of the law.</note>

After that, the Lord <term>Sâkyamuni</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., rose from his pulpit, gathered the <term>Bodhisattvas</term>, took their right hands with his own right hand—which had become strong by the exercise of magic—and spoke on that occasion as follows: "Into your hands, young men of good family, I transfer and transmit, entrust and deposit this supreme and perfect enlightenment attained by me after hundreds of thousands of myriads of <term>kotis</term> of incalculable <term>Aeons</term>. You, young men of good family, do your best so that it may grow and spread."

A second time and a third time, the Lord spoke to the host of <term>Bodhisattvas</term> after taking them by their right hands: "Into your hands, young men of good family, I transfer and transmit, entrust and deposit this supreme and perfect enlightenment attained by me after hundreds of thousands of myriads of <term>kotis</term> of incalculable <term>Aeons</term>. Receive it, young men of good family; keep, read, understand deeply, teach, proclaim, and preach it to all beings. I am not greedy, young men of good family, nor narrow-minded; I am confident and willing to impart Buddha-knowledge, to impart the knowledge of the <term>Tathâgata</term>, the knowledge of the Self-born. I am a bountiful giver, young"

<summary>In the final chapter, Buddha Sâkyamuni ceremonially entrusts the mission of spreading supreme enlightenment to the Bodhisattvas. He encourages them to preach the Dharma to all beings, emphasizing his own lack of greed and his desire to share universal Buddha-knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Sâkyamuni, Tathâgata, Bodhisattvas, enlightenment, kotis, Aeons, Dharmaparyâya, Buddha-knowledge, Self-born, entrustment</keywords>

--- Page 487 ---
<meta>This page continues the conclusion of Chapter XXVII, where Lord Sâkyamuni completes his entrustment of the Dharma to the Bodhisattvas and dismisses the gathered assembly.</meta>

<page-num>441</page-num>
<header>XXVII. THE PERIOD.</header>

Men of good family, and you, young men of good family, follow my example; imitate me in liberally showing this knowledge of the <term>Tathâgata</term>, and in skillfulness, and preach this <term>Dharmaparyâya</term> to the young men and young ladies of good family who successively shall gather around you. And as for unbelieving persons, rouse them to accept this law. By doing so, young men of good family, you will repay your debt to the <term>Tathâgatas</term>.

So addressed by the Lord <term>Sâkyamuni</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> were filled with delight and joy, and with a feeling of great respect they lowered, bent, and bowed their bodies toward the Lord; with heads inclined and joined hands stretched out, they spoke in one voice to the Lord <term>Sâkyamuni</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., with the following words: "We shall do, O Lord, what the <term>Tathâgata</term> commands; we shall fulfill the command of all <term>Tathâgatas</term>. Let the Lord be at ease regarding this, and perfectly quiet." A second time, and a third time, the entire host of <term>Bodhisattvas</term> spoke in one voice the same words: "Let the Lord be at ease regarding this, and perfectly quiet. We shall do, O Lord, what the <term>Tathâgata</term> commands us; we shall fulfill the command of all <term>Tathâgatas</term>."

Thereupon the Lord <term>Sâkyamuni</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., dismissed all those <term>Tathâgatas</term>, etc., who had come to the gathering from other worlds, and wished them a happy existence with the words: "May the <term>Tathâgatas</term>, etc., live happily." Then he restored the <term>Stûpa</term> of precious substances of the Lord <term>Prabhûtaratna</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., to its place, and wished him also a happy existence.

Thus spoke the Lord. The incalculable, innumerable <term>Tathâgatas</term>, etc., who had come from other

<vocab>Tathâgata, Dharmaparyâya, Sâkyamuni, Bodhisattva, Stûpa, Prabhûtaratna</vocab>

<summary>Lord Sâkyamuni instructs the Bodhisattvas to spread the Buddha-knowledge to all, including unbelievers, as a way to repay their debt to the Tathâgatas. The Bodhisattvas joyfully accept the mission, after which the Buddha dismisses the visiting deities and restores the Stûpa of Prabhûtaratna.</summary>
<keywords>Sâkyamuni, Bodhisattvas, Dharmaparyâya, Prabhûtaratna, Stûpa, missionary command, dismissal of the assembly</keywords>

<header>SADDHARMA-PUNDARÎKA. XXVII.</header>

worlds and were sitting on their thrones at the foot of jewel trees, as well as <term>Prabhûtaratna</term>, the <term>Tathâgata</term>, etc., and the whole host of <term>Bodhisattvas</term> headed by <term>Visishtakâritra</term>, the innumerable, incalculable <term>Bodhisattvas Mahâsattvas</term> who had emerged from the gaps of the earth, the great disciples, the four classes, and the world—including gods, men, demons, and <term>Gandharvas</term>—in ecstasy applauded the words of the Lord.
